On her way, she sent the temple priest to the house to tell the children to stop making noise and to close the doors.

The children were lost in their dance. They had forgotten the world around them. Even though Shyam’s mother called out to them several times, her words did not reach their ears. Finally, she called out sternly, “Shyam!” At once, Shyam’s eyes fell on his mother. The banging of tins stopped abruptly. She asked angrily, “What is going on here?”

“Bhajan, Mother! Didn’t you yourself give us the Shaligram? We are singing bhajans in front of it. Why are you angry with us?” Just then, the priest arrived. He told them to close the doors and said that the noise was disturbing the Purana recital.
“No, we won’t stop. Just as you have your Purana, we have our bhajan,” said one stubborn child.
Shyam’s mother tried to explain to Shyam, “Shyam, can’t you sing bhajans quietly? Why do you need to bang the tins? When you sing bhajans, you must not make such a racket with the doors and tins.”
“There is no need. If your actions cause trouble to others, what kind of devotion is that?”
“Don’t saints and holy men sing bhajans and play the cymbals?” asked Shyam.
“Listen, Shyam, they never do anything that would trouble others. Is it more important to take God’s name, or to make noise?” said Aai.
“But it’s not fun unless we make some noise,” said Shyam.

“If you really want to make music, then go out to the fields and keep your rhythm there. Making noise is not important. When you worship God, when you pray, you must make sure that it does not trouble others. If you do this, your bhajan can go on, and the recitation in the temple can continue as well. No one will be disturbed,” said Aai.

She recited a proverb to the children and sent the priest back. Shyam understood what Aai had said. Some of the children did not agree. One mischievous boy said, “Shyam, you’re such a coward!” “What’s cowardly about this?” Shyam replied. “I believe what Aai said. To act accordingly is the real mark of courage.” Shyam explained to the other boys. But they did not agree. All of them left, angry with Shyam. Shyam was left alone. He began to cry, and sat in the temple, singing bhajans to God.
Shyam grew older. Then he said, “Now everyone has left me, and I am left all alone.” On this, Shyam recalled the words of Rabindranath Tagore:

“You are destined to walk alone. Take your lamp and walk on. The winds of criticism from others may come and threaten to extinguish your lamp. But you must light it again and keep moving forward. You are destined to walk alone.”
Isn’t it true?
chapters.summary: When young Shyam's boisterous devotional drumming disrupts the temple Purana, his mother gently teaches him that true devotion considers the peace and feelings of others.

chapters.title: If I Had Run Away
paragraphs: In Maharashtra, Wai is a sacred place. It lies on the banks of the Krishna river. During the month of Kanyagat, many people come to bathe in the Krishna. There is a belief that during this time, the northern river Ganga comes to meet the Krishna. Because of this, crowds upon crowds of people come on pilgrimage. People from Palgad also travel there. In those days, there were no cars or trains like today. People traveled in bullock carts during those years.
There was such a pilgrimage then.

Some people from Palgad were planning to go. Shyam’s paternal uncle and aunt, and some villagers, were preparing for the journey. Ten or twelve bullock carts were arranged for the trip. Along the way, they would stop, rest, cook and eat, and then continue their journey. Shyam loved such journeys. Because on such trips, the mind becomes one with nature. At night, the stars shine brightly in the sky. The sound of the bells around the necks of the bullocks is sweet to the ears.

Since childhood, Shyam had loved to worship. When he saw these people preparing, he too wanted to go with them. From the moment he heard about the trip to Wai, he began to pester his mother. He insisted on going, behaving stubbornly, as children do. He pleaded his case, praised the merits of the pilgrimage, and tried to make his mother understand, “Our situation—

We never have enough money to give you, my child. If you truly wish to go, then go. Have I ever stopped you from going anywhere because of money? Krishna himself would not have been Krishna if he had not obeyed his parents. Do you know what happened to Pundalik? Even when God himself came, he kept him waiting at his feet!"

"But Dhruva left his parents and went into the forest to do penance, didn’t he? And anyway, is it always necessary to do exactly what comes to mind? And who ran away in the end? When uncle told him, he returned home quietly," Shyam replied to his mother, defending himself. To this, his mother said, "Taking money from them is their greatness. But for us, it is a matter of shame. Why should we burden them? People worship God with others’ wealth. One should work hard oneself, earn oneself, and then offer it to God. If you really want to go, then go on foot."
"But I have to go far, don’t I? Is it possible to travel such a long distance on foot?" Shyam expressed his doubt.

"Now you are telling me about Dhruva? Was he not afraid? Did he not think about how he would survive in the forest? Whoever sets out towards God, God helps him in every way. Do you have the same faith as Dhruva?" his mother asked.

Hearing this, Shyam began to cry. "Shyam, why are you crying? Are you afraid, my child? We are simple people. You are still young. We are poor. We must not insist on things we cannot afford," his mother tried to console him.

Yet, Shyam could not be satisfied. The thought of not being able to go on the pilgrimage weighed heavily on his mind. Thinking about it late into the night, he finally fell asleep. When he woke up in the morning...

Everyone had gone on the pilgrimage. In a hurry, Shyam washed his face, bathed, performed his morning prayers, offered water to the tulsi plant, and, taking his slate and books, set off towards school.
“Shyam, come here, my dear. Eat something and then go. No one else has gone to school yet,” Mother called out.
“I don’t want to eat. Why don’t you let me go to school early? I am hungry to study, not to eat. I’ll go and sit in school,” Shyam replied, a little angrily.

“Later, when you want to eat, don’t come to me! I’m telling you now! Everything must go your way, mustn’t it? You’re a real prince! If only you’d been born in a royal family, it would have been fine. What’s the use of being born in a poor home and acting like a king? Don’t want to eat, you say? Did you ever get food whenever you wanted? How many days have you stayed hungry? Shyam, listen to what I say, listen to your mother,” Mother said, a little sternly.

But Shyam paid no attention to her scolding. He went to school. No one else had arrived yet. He put his books on the bench and, unable to sit still, began to pace up and down, eager to study. But after a while, he started to feel faint. There was no sign of the bullock carts. He felt like crying. He didn’t want to go home, nor did he want to wander in the fields—he was in such a state. At last, he wandered along the deserted paths, feeling utterly forlorn. His stomach growled with hunger. He returned to the village, but felt ashamed to go home. His pride held him back. One part of him said, “Why show such pride to your mother and father? That’s an insult to their love!” There was a temple in the village. In that temple, in a dark corner beside a torn curtain...
I sat there, subdued and silent. But how long could I remain sitting? Eventually, gathering myself, I started to make my way home.

By then, school had ended. The children brought Shyam’s satchel home for him. That’s when the family at home realized Shyam hadn’t returned. On the very first day, Shyam’s handwriting exercise had gone badly, and the headmaster had punished him. Everyone assumed that, frightened by the punishment, Shyam had run away from home. The headmaster was worried. Shyam’s father came to the school to inquire. Seeing the fear of punishment, it seemed to him that Shyam must have run away. In truth, Shyam’s father had always urged him to improve his handwriting, making him practice every day. He was a little annoyed with the headmaster for this. The headmaster told him not to scold the boy any further. “Let it be for now! Let him come home!” said Shyam’s father. Still, a faint doubt lingered in his mother’s heart—what if Shyam had indeed run away? But she did not let it show.

No one at home had eaten or even had a snack. Father, uncle, and the neighbors all set out to look for Shyam. As Shyam was returning home, his uncle spotted him. He took Shyam by the hand and brought him home. Many children had gathered to watch him being brought back. Shyam’s father told all the children to go home now.

Father was not angry with Shyam. He understood him. “There’s no need to act like this just because the master scolded you. In our days, punishments were even harsher. If the master says so, a beating is part of it,” he explained, and then asked Shyam’s mother to give him something to eat.
Shyam got up, washed his hands and feet. He did not mention that his clothes were torn because of the master’s beating.

Hearing about the beating, he felt consoled. He ate his meal. It was Saturday. There was no school. Even as the afternoon wore on, he did not wake up. Mother came and sat by his pillow. She gently stroked his forehead with her hand. She called out softly to Shyam, “Shyam.” He woke up. Mother was sitting beside him. One of her hands rested on his body. She said, “Shyam, are you feeling better? Does your body ache? Did you hear what I told you?” Saying this, she began to caress his body.

Shyam began to cry. He put his head on his mother’s lap and started sobbing. He said to her, “Aai, I listened to what you said. I ran away. Are you angry with me? The master beat me, so I ran away. But have you ever beaten me? When you told me to walk with your own feet, I went away in anger. But now I realize that was wrong. Who is Dhruva and who is Shyam! Your Shyam is stubborn. Once something comes into my mind, I rush to do it. If I can’t, I get upset and start crying. Aai, are you angry with me? Tell me the truth!”

She took him in her arms. She stroked his face with her hand and began to speak, “Shyam, I am not angry with you. When you didn’t come home, I was afraid. I felt that I was to blame for all this. I felt bad that you ran away. But you didn’t run away for any bad reason, did you? You didn’t run away from God, did you? You didn’t go to hide from Krishna, did you? If you had run away from God, I would have felt ashamed to say it! Remember just this one thing I tell you: never run away after stealing or doing wrong. Never run away after keeping bad company. Never run away out of fear. All the saints ran away only to be closer to God. If you ever run away, let it be only towards God. For that, I will pray to God for you.”
chapters.summary: After a harsh school punishment and missing the pilgrimage, a hungry and forlorn Shyam returns home, confessing to his mother about running away in anger.

chapters.title: Work Hard and Succeed
paragraphs: Since his childhood, Shyam had a fondness for reading. He would read books like *Harivijay* and *Mahavijay*. Except for one or two hymns, he did not know Sanskrit. He was a devotee of Rama. There was a neighbor of his age, named Bhaskar. Bhaskar would recite the *Ramraksha* hymn, which was in Sanskrit. He had memorized the entire *Ramraksha*. Shyam could not do so. Though he too was a devotee of Rama, he felt ashamed that he could not recite it.

Bhaskar had a copy of the *Ramraksha*. Every evening, he would come to Shyam and recite the verses of the *Ramraksha* to him. Hearing this, Shyam would feel a surge of anger. Bhaskar could recite the *Ramraksha*, but he himself could not—this made him feel embarrassed. It seemed to him that Bhaskar was reciting the verses deliberately to tease him. This pained him. He would get angry at Bhaskar.
One day, as usual, Bhaskar came over. He said to Shyam, “Shyam, only ten verses remain for me to memorize. In five or six days, I will have memorized the entire *Ramraksha*.”

Hearing this, Shyam slapped him. He realized that he was telling on him. He ran straight to Bhaskar’s courtyard and blocked his way, saying, “Bhashya, don’t show off. Enough of your cleverness. If I had a book, I would have learned and shown you. Who are you to show off to? And if you come to our house and show off again, you’ll see what happens!”

Hearing the commotion outside, Mother came out. She asked, “Bhaskar, what’s all this noise? Shyam, did you hit him?” Bhaskar explained what had happened. Then she turned to Shyam and asked, “What is this, Shyam? Did you really say that? Is this how you behave with neighbors? Should you act like this with your friends?”
Shyam’s anger had not yet cooled. He replied angrily, “He teases me on purpose. He says I don’t know the Ramraksha, and he teases me on purpose. He’s always showing off.”

Mother tried to reason with Shyam, “If he said you don’t know the Ramraksha, what’s so wrong in that? Why get angry when someone points out a shortcoming in us? Instead, seeing that shortcoming, Bhaskar wants you to learn the Ramraksha by heart. Why don’t you memorize it?”
“My brother gets to study, but where do I have a book?” Shyam answered his mother’s question.
“Take Bhaskar’s book and memorize it. If not, take the book and make a copy of it,” Mother said.

Bhaskar went home. Shyam decided firmly in his heart that he would copy down the Ramraksha from the neighbor’s book and memorize it. He told no one. He got paper and pen ready. He waited for the evening light. Early in the morning, Shyam went to Bhaskar’s house. When Bhaskar was not at home, Shyam went straight to his mother. “Bhima-tai, may I have the book for a while?”
Did Bhaskara give you the Ramraksha book? I want to memorize the Ramraksha. Isn’t today a holiday? I thought I’d spend the whole day sitting and finishing it,” Shyama said softly.

Bhima-tai glanced at Bhaskara and told him to give Shyama the Ramraksha book. At first, he wasn’t ready to give it. But before his anger could rise, she handed it over. Shyama took it and came home. He began to memorize the Ramraksha. By afternoon, he had memorized a good portion of it. After lunch, he sat down again. When the work was finally done, how happy Shyama was! He felt satisfied. In those days, there were few printing presses. Because of that, handwritten books were common. Preparing them took a lot of effort. Now, there are plenty of printing presses. Books are easily available. But who strives to acquire knowledge? Life has become easier, people have grown, honesty and a sense of duty have increased in people’s hearts. Sacrifice and love—these qualities, it seems, are still present in people.

Shyama gave Bhaskara the Ramraksha book back, just as he had received it. Bhima-tai took the handwritten copy and checked it. She tested him on it. She told Shyama to memorize the Ramraksha. Shyama came home and sat down to memorize it. Now, he no longer wasted time. He kept at it, memorizing the Ramraksha. By the next day, he had memorized the whole Ramraksha. Before Bapu returned in the evening, he was eager to recite it to him.

Bapu came home. He washed his hands and feet and entered the house. He asked Shyama, “Tell me, what is the Shubhamkaroti verse?” Shyama replied, “Brother, I have learned all of it. Won’t you listen to the Ramraksha now?”
Hearing this, Bapu was surprised. He asked, “Oh! Who taught you? When did you memorize it?”

Shyam told everything to his father. Father asked Shyam to show him the handwriting of the Ramraksha he had copied. Shyam brought it and showed it to him. Father looked at it carefully, guided him on how to write the letters better, and showed him the right way to improve. Shyam recited the Ramraksha. Father affectionately ran his hand over Shyam’s head. Shyam was overjoyed. He could not find words to describe that happiness.

Everyone finished their meal. Shyam went to his mother in the cowshed. He recited the Ramraksha to her and said, “Aai, how was my Ramraksha? I was angry with you, but still, I showed you my Ramraksha first, didn’t I?”

“I knew you had copied the Ramraksha well,” she said. “I was eager to see your handwriting. But I also knew you would come and show it to me. I was waiting for you since the evening. You should always come and show me whatever good you do first. Just as I get angry when you do something wrong, I am just as delighted when you do something good. A mother’s joy is in her child’s virtues. How much happiness a mother feels when her child learns something good! Did you keep this happiness hidden from me for eight days? Let that be! Now, have you memorized the Ramraksha? If you don’t have the book, will you just sit and cry? God has given everyone a mind, hands, feet, intelligence—everything. You must make use of them. Work hard and become great. Never depend on others. Stand on your own feet. Remember one thing: just because you know a lot, never look down on others. Share what you have with others. Treat them as your own.” She explained this to Shyam.

She took the Ramraksha book in her hands. She was very happy. She said to Shyam, “There is a picture of Rama in the cloth shop at the market. Get it from someone. Keep it in your notebook. It will look nice. Today, you have pleased God very much, because you worked hard and did all this. You have memorized it.”
chapters.summary: After a confrontation with Bhaskar, Shyam, spurred by his mother's wisdom, secretly copies the Ramraksha, determined to prove his dedication and make his parents proud.

chapters.title: Who is Wasteful?
paragraphs: There is a certain culture, a tradition, in the way we eat. Shyam’s father would always tell Shyam to finish his meal on his own plate. While eating, one must not pick from others’ plates first! One must not be greedy. Do not leave food on your plate. Do not speak ill of the food that has been served to you. If you find a stone or anything odd in the food, quietly remove it without making a fuss, but if it is something harmful, then you must tell your mother. Shyam’s father himself followed these rules. After he finished eating, his plate would be so clean that it was hard to tell whether anyone had eaten from it at all. There would not be a single grain of rice left around his plate. Similarly, if any grains of rice fell around the children’s plates, they were made to gather them all together. Never once did anyone complain about the food served. If someone asked, “How was it?” and the answer was “Excellent,” only then was it considered good. There was never any mischief at mealtime.

Let me tell you about one such day. After performing the daily worship at home, Shyam’s father went to the Ganpati temple, while Shyam and his siblings sat down to eat. They left only the rice on their plates, eating everything else. When their father returned—

As soon as I appeared, mother would tell me to go and wash my hands and feet. When Bapu returned, he would bring holy water with him, and after distributing that holy water to everyone, the meal would begin.

Shyam’s mother was an excellent cook. Whatever vegetable she prepared, it always tasted delicious when made by her hands. Her hands were truly the hands of Annapurna herself! Whatever she did, she did with all her heart. When the heart is sweet, everything becomes sweet and tastes sweet. That day, she had made leafy greens—Shyam’s favorite. But mother forgot to add salt. In the rush of chores, she simply forgot. Yet, no one said a word while eating. Bapu didn’t say anything, nor did the children. No one reached for the salt to sprinkle on their plate. “How is the vegetable?” Bapu asked. “It’s good,” I replied. Since it was Shyam’s favorite vegetable, Bapu asked him, and Shyam gave the same answer as his father. “Now that he’s started learning English, he doesn’t like these vegetables anymore!” Bapu teased.
“If learning English is going to make me worse, then why do you want me to study?” Shyam retorted.

“I only said it to tease you. You look nice when you get angry. Don’t you like the taste of cucumber flowers? Sometimes I eat even the tough ones. If the vegetable is old, make it at home,” Bapu said.

Mother nodded in agreement. Thus, the meal passed in good spirits. Bapu got up, washed his face, and went outside. There, he began his hundred paces while reciting the Vishnusahasranama. After he left, mother sat down to spin thread. When everyone had finished eating, Shyam’s mother finally sat down to her meal. As soon as she put the vegetable in her mouth, she realized it was bland—she had forgotten to add salt. Shyam was still sitting nearby. She asked him, “Shyam, was there salt in the vegetable?”
Let it be! Why didn’t you tell anyone about it? How did you eat the bland curry?"
“Brother, I did tell you, didn’t I? Didn’t I say it?” Shyam replied.

She felt very bad. While everyone else said nothing, she felt deeply hurt that Shyam mentioned the curry was bland. Shyam did not take back his words, and even then, she wished he would realize it himself; but how could he have known? So she remained restless.

She saw clearly that she had made a big mistake. Her nature was always to do well whatever she did for others. She had erred in her work. Not taking care to add salt was not right, she kept thinking, and so she remained troubled.

She did not want anyone to feel bad, so Bapu also stayed quiet. After all the trouble she took to prepare the meal, it should have been eaten with sweetness, and no fault should have been found; one should not hurt the feelings of the one who cooked, that is what Bapu thought. Only when something is said without thinking does it hurt so much, and when one realizes this, the impact is even greater.

Shyam says, “Who is at fault? Is it me, Aai? One should not hurt another’s feelings, so we must control our tongue. If the curry needed salt, I could have said so gently, or if I had made something myself, I should have taken care to do it right. Why should I be restless or complain? Both are at fault! Hindu culture stands on restraint and contentment. It is also founded on skill in action. These two lessons—restraint and skill—my Aai and Bapu gave me.”
All this Shyam told himself, and thus he learned a great lesson.
chapters.summary: When Shyam's mother realizes she forgot salt in the leafy greens, she is hurt that Shyam mentioned it was bland.

chapters.title: Why Live in the World?
paragraphs: When Shyam had to go to Pune to study, he stayed at his maternal uncle's house. At that time, he was about eleven years old. His uncle was, by nature, a short-tempered man. Shyam had to endure many scoldings and punishments there. He was often beaten for small mistakes, and his mind grew weary of staying there. Two or three times, he even ran away from his uncle’s house. Once, he went to Mumbai. Another time, he came back home. Finally, his uncle, fed up with all this trouble, said, "Enough of this nuisance here," and sent Shyam back home.

When he returned home, his father had just been released from prison. He had been imprisoned during the Swadeshi movement. His health was not good, so he was staying at a relative’s house. Shyam’s elder sister had been married and had come home to her parental house. She had a little daughter, still an infant, who was being breastfed. The sister had come home but soon fell seriously ill. She was struck with a severe attack of typhoid. At home, only Aai was there. She had to manage all the household chores by herself. Shyam...

Payan Akka was unable to give her own child any milk. That milk, tainted by her illness, had become poisonous. Because of it, the little child suffered greatly. At such a time, Shyam returned home from Pune. Mama sent him home instead of letting him stay with him. Who had the leisure to pay attention to him then? On the contrary, all the affection in the house was reserved for Akka. She was wasting away day by day. Her illness kept growing worse. One day, she began to burn with fever. She started rambling incessantly. In her delirium, she spoke of everything that had happened to her since she came into the house. So much money had been spent on her wedding. Akka had been the darling of all. Hearing of her suffering made my mother’s heart ache terribly.

There were many faults among us. Brothers would quarrel among themselves, and in drunkenness, would be sent home. The daughters-in-law and daughters of the house would trouble everyone. Truly, if one were to speak plainly, mothers-in-law and mothers would have to leave the house and go to their own parents. Or, in anger, they would have to leave the family altogether. But such a thing was never seen to happen. On the contrary, when a daughter-in-law entered the house, she became just another member of the household! Mothers-in-law would trouble their daughters-in-law. But when that same daughter-in-law became a mother-in-law herself, she would forget the hardships she had once endured and would trouble her own daughter-in-law in turn. Just as a teacher scolds his students, and when that student grows up to be a teacher, he does the same. Even in simple games, we notice this same pattern. Therefore, both the school and the home must be reformed. Our culture is very deep-rooted. It teaches us to love trees and plants, animals and birds, even insects and worms. But in practice, we...
How hard-hearted some people are, this becomes evident at such times.

After the meal at Danapara, everyone sat together in the courtyard. Among them, three women sat with brass pots filled with cold water in their hands. They waited for Aai to call them to fetch water or to assign them some other task. But Aai, telling Shyam to keep an eye on things, got up and went to the temple. There, she prayed to God. She told God what needed to be done. Both effort and prayer went hand in hand. Day and night, Aai’s service continued without pause. God’s cooperation is needed along with effort. All the time, Aai was busy with work; she was alone at home. She had to do all the chores by herself. It was evening. Rangu and Shyam were playing. But soon, Rangu came running, crying, to Aai. She kept weeping continuously. It seemed she was upset about something necessary or about some work she had to do. She had to tie the calf, milk the cow, light the lamp, grind the grain, and do many such chores. She was completely absorbed in her work. Two hands were not enough for her. Who else but a woman can bear such hardship? If one could see the hardships borne by women, one would see goddesses not only in temples but also in homes. Aai was busy with her work, and it was not possible for Akka to go to the temple. Rangu could not go to the temple for Aai’s sake either. In such circumstances, Rangu’s heart was troubled, and she began to cry. She wept and wailed loudly. But her crying did not reach Aai’s ears. Only a certain measure of patience remains. Hearing Rangu’s crying, Aai lost her temper. In that moment of anger, she said, “Where did you go, child? Just stop crying. No work gets done by crying.”
“Shyam, hold her, she’s crying—”

How could I sleep after that! Did I even get up or not! Then, the storm of Appurbai’s words and virtues kept swirling in my mind, refusing to die down. How many times must you die for someone else’s faults? Were you born just to suffer for others?'' Aunt stormed off in anger, muttering as she went.

Shyam listened to all this. Those sharp words pierced his heart. He felt like crying. Just like that, he got up, took his prayer beads, and went outside. He began to recite shlokas and the Ramraksha. While playing with Rangoo, he gently rocked him to sleep on his shoulder. When Rangoo fell asleep, Shyam’s mind became alert and awake. Why does one live in this world? He began to understand. Only a virtuous person seems to have a place in the world. What use is a person without virtues? A useless stick is of no use to anyone. On the contrary, such a life becomes a burden upon others! From that day on, Shyam’s life found a new path. It is true what they say—that the time for change comes when it is meant to come!
Shyam prayed to God, ''O God! I will try to become wise for my mother’s sake. Give me strength for this resolve! Be pleased with me! Make me virtuous and make Akka well again.''

From that day onwards, Akka began to recover. She became completely well. She was restored to health, and Shyam’s mind too found peace. It was as if both of them had been given a new life. Akka received a new body, and Shyam, a new mind.
chapters.summary: After hearing harsh words, Shyam wanders outside with prayer beads, questioning his purpose and resolving to become virtuous for his mother's sake and Akka's health.

chapters.title: True Beauty Lies in Virtue
paragraphs: After bringing Shyam back from Pune, Mama decided to enroll him in the Mission School at Dapoli so that he could improve his English. Dapoli is a beautiful town, about six kos from Palgad. If you walk, it takes half a day to reach there. Arrangements were made for Shyam to stay at the house of a certain Rao in Dapoli. There, a distant aunt also lived. Shyam stayed with them. Their circumstances were poor. They had to manage with very little for food and drink. Life was lived with great care and frugality.
The school itself was good. There was a teacher named Namne. Shyam liked the school very much. The atmosphere there was pleasant. Shyam was content.
From childhood, Shyam was accustomed to a little hardship.

In this world, there are times when one feels as if one has no one of their own. At such moments, tears come to the eyes. It is only in childhood that one sees the need to receive love and sympathy. If a person gets food for a while, he can survive; but if he does not receive love, he cannot truly live. Love is life itself. Shyam always felt a deep hunger for love. He would be reminded of his home again and again. When Saturday came, he would eagerly wait for school to end in the afternoon, and before the last bell rang, he would rush outside, longing to go home. By evening, he would reach home. His mother would be there, waiting for him. During the time he spent at home, he would receive the love of his mother and of everyone else. It was on the strength of this love that he would pass the coming days. In those days, his hunger for love was immense. When a person has to live away from home, he truly understands the value of the love he receives at home.

So, one Saturday, Shyam set out for home. He could hardly wait to reach. He was hungry for the loving atmosphere of his home. In childhood, children long to receive love. Only when one grows older does one understand the true importance of love. There is great satisfaction in giving love as well as receiving it. But when one is young, it is more important to receive it. A person gives only what he has received.

As he walked, memories of home flooded his mind. He wanted to cry. Tears welled up in his eyes from time to time as he walked. The path led through fields and woods. In the beginning, he had been afraid to take this path...

He felt afraid. But, taking God’s name, he pressed on with determination. On the way, he grew thirsty. At a certain well, he drank some water. Before darkness could fall, he hurried along, eager to reach home.

When he arrived, the lamps in the house were already lit. His younger brother was reciting shlokas. Mother was busy preparing dinner. The little siblings, overjoyed at Shyam’s return, ran to him—“Anna’s here! Anna’s here!” they cried, dancing around him.
“Why did you stay out so late? Didn’t you come home much later than usual? It’s already night, child,” Mother said, her words full of concern.
“I couldn’t walk any further, Mother. I felt so weak, I couldn’t go on,” Shyam replied.
“If you couldn’t go on, why did you come at all? You could have waited and come home after Sankranti,” Mother said.

“Mother, I came just to see you. When you call me with love, it gives my heart new strength. I have come back carrying that strength,” he said, and then, unable to hold back, he flung himself into his mother’s arms and began to weep. Tears filled Mother’s eyes too. The little siblings also began to cry. Mother wiped her own eyes, then wiped Shyam’s tears. She rubbed oil onto his tired feet, and brought warm water to wash them. As Mother massaged his feet with oil, Shyam drifted into a trance, experiencing a unique, tender feeling of love. She washed his feet, and then, as he sat down to eat,

I came inside the house and sat down. My younger siblings were being taught shlokas with great care. Just then, Shyam’s father entered the house. He had just returned from the fields. Looking at his face, it was clear that he was weary and troubled. Shyam’s usual cheerful greeting did not bring a smile to his father’s face today. He washed his feet and sat down to perform his evening prayers. He noticed that Shyam had not done his own prayers yet. With irritation, he said to Shyam, “Shyam, why are you sitting here? Why are you hanging around the kitchen like the women? Go and do your prayers!” Mother spoke up in his defense, “He just came back inside, so he sat down.” She then told Shyam to go and do his prayers. Shyam felt hurt. He did his prayers, but as he did, tears welled up in his eyes.

Afterwards, his father called him over and said, “Don’t you have any work to do? And why have you let your hair grow so long? Don’t you know how to keep yourself neat? Didn’t your mother tell you to get your hair cut when you had the time? Are you planning to grow horns now? Tomorrow morning, take some money from your mother and go get your hair cut. If you don’t, don’t come back here. Go on now!”

With hope for affection, Shyam had come home. But instead, these harsh words made him want to cry. Seeing this, his father asked again, “Why are you crying? Who hit you? Behave yourself!” Mother intervened and said, “Tomorrow, he’ll get his hair cut. You give him the money.”
Did you bathe in the pond? You don’t have any money with him, do you? And don’t waste your time either. Isn’t there a school in the village?” Thus, she explained things to Shyam.
She told his father to offer prayers to God. In the words of both parents, Shyam saw two guiding lights. The nectar from his mother’s lips overflowed.
Shyam experienced the monsoon and the winter.

Everyone finished their meal. Mother served Shyam a little extra of his favorite dish, just for him. Unnoticed, Shyam gave that extra portion to his younger brother. The joy he felt in giving it to him was immense. The sweetness of giving food to his little brother was greater than the satisfaction he had ever felt when he himself was given money.

Everyone finished their chores and went to bed. Shyam found a place for himself at the edge of the bed. While working, his mother deliberately called him over. She made him lie down to sleep. She sang lullabies to him as she patted him to sleep. While listening, Shyam said to his mother, “Aai, I want to leave this house. How much my brother troubles me! When I go to the fields, I want to leave before he comes.”

Hearing these words from Shyam, she gently explained to him, “Shyam, don’t ever think of leaving your brother behind. Even if he sometimes misbehaves, let it go. Our situation is not good right now. Even so, your father takes loans so you children can study. He wears old, patched clothes himself. He works hard to feed you, his little ones. He toils for you. How can you be angry with him?
Why not die? If you go astray for the sake of your hair, who will recognize you in the future? Mother—
Are you not ready to cut your hair just to look good? Why do you let such vain feelings trouble you?"
"What religion is there in hair and such things?" Shyam asked.

"There is religion in every little thing. What you eat, what you drink, there is religion in everything. Why did you grow your hair? You have become attached to your hair. Give up that attachment, and that is religion!" Mother tried to explain.

Though Mother could not fully explain it to Shyam at that moment, as life went on, Shyam understood all of this. To think carefully about every action, to do only what is true, beneficial, and auspicious—that alone is religion. There is religion in every act, this is the truth. He had grown his hair to look handsome. But true beauty lies in virtue; it lies in purity—he realized this later. If Mother had only given Shyam love, she would have shown him the right path.

In the morning, Shyam called the barber and had his hair cut. He bathed. On his way back, he brought a small plate. He brought turmeric leaves. Mother told Shyam to make a plate out of the leaves for water. She liked that. Then she told Shyam to collect firewood and give it to the cook. She told Shyam that from now on, he should fast once every fifteen days for Ekadashi. Hearing all these sweet instructions, Shyam’s heart was filled with joy. Bapuya, from his own share—

While doing all this, he felt ashamed of his earlier stubbornness. When he thought of getting angry at them, he realized how wrong it would have been. Even his father’s love, which came in its own way, now seemed precious to him. He understood how petty it was to feel anger just because of a few words spoken by his father. Shyam realized his own shortcomings.

He gathered flowers for the worship—tulsi, bel leaves, and blades of durva grass. He made all the preparations for the puja. After that, he began to help with whatever work was needed. He swept the courtyard, wiped the turmeric leaves, and helped prepare the tavasli.

Father finished his worship and came in. The meal was ready. The leaves were set for everyone. All the family members ate with great satisfaction. Shyam was especially content. He insisted that his father eat the tavasli. Even when his father spoke harshly, he had never actually beaten him. He only insisted on getting some work done, that was all.

While talking, Mother said to Shyam, “Shyam, if you had run away and gone today, do you know how bad your brothers would have felt? Food would not have tasted sweet to them. They love you very much. I am never well enough to go and look after them.

If I am forced to leave them alone, I feel terrible. Even though they have brothers and sisters, who will care for them? You must always look after them. If ever they are in trouble, you must help them. You must give them happiness.”
Mother ate her meal. All the work was done. The brothers and the little ones...
They sat together and played. Mother gave Shyam a little piece of cloth to sew ahead. Then she told him a beautiful story. The day passed by in this way.

Shyam woke up early in the morning and bathed. Mother had her meal. Shyam finished his meal and then fell at his mother’s feet. She asked him to come home for Sankranti. If his legs hurt, she told him to come by cart. She blessed him with deep affection. She asked him not to hold any anger in his heart towards his brother, but to forgive him. She told him to study well and to take care of his younger siblings.

That day, I set out from home towards Dapoli. Father walked a little way with me to see me off. After that, Shyam started walking alone. Earlier, when he arrived at the house in Dapoli, he would cry because he missed the love of home. But now, having received so much love from the people of Dapoli, his heart would be so full that he would feel like crying again. One weeps in sorrow, and one also weeps in happiness. Now, Shyam’s heart overflowed with happiness, and tears came to his eyes. Remembering the love of his family, he felt moved to tears.
chapters.summary: After a long walk home, Shyam is eager to see his family, but his father's harsh words about his appearance leave Shyam hurt and confused.

chapters.title: Who is to Blame for Mistakes?
paragraphs: There was an old woman named Dwarakakaku who used to stay at Shyama’s house. During the time of sharing the harvest, she would come and stay with them. Her brother—Shyama’s father—would be busy working in the fields, tending to the rice crop. None of them were idle. Her brother’s nature was such that she trusted him completely.

The children had given her a nickname—Durva Aaji, the Grandmother of Sacred Grass. During the holy months of Chaturmas, women would offer sacred grass (durva) and flowers to the gods. From morning itself, women would come to her for durva. She considered serving the gods as her duty.
“Where has Aaji gone? Aaji has gone to pluck durva,” the children would say. And so, she came to be known as Durva Aaji.

She had many virtues. Every morning, she would draw water from the well with her own hands and give it to others. She never complained of any hardship. At night, she would guard the fields all alone. If someone’s body ached, she would apply oil and relieve their pain. If the children fell ill, she would tend to them. If someone suffered from fever, she would give them advice. She would fetch water from the well for those in need. Her hands were blessed with healing power. When Shyama’s eyes troubled him, she would always rub his feet with the sacred cow’s ghee. She cared for everyone in the house and the courtyard.
This is how people’s help is sometimes rendered.

Aaji (grandmother) had connections with all the families in the neighborhood. She played games with the children. She attended the Mangala Gauri gatherings. She would go wherever there were games being played. Songs of different women would be heard there.

Aaji would help Shyam’s mother a little as needed. She would cut the vegetables and give them. She played with the little children. If there was grinding to be done, she would lend a hand. But by nature, she was whimsical. It was hard to say when she might get upset.

One day, assuming that Aaji would help, Shyam’s mother decided to prepare the flour mixture and set things up for grinding. She told Aaji about it. But that very morning, an invitation came from a neighbor for a special occasion—someone in the family was making payasam, and Aaji was invited. She was, after all, the village grandmother. She would be specially called for making papads and pickles. She would spend the whole day there, eating and chatting, and return in the evening. That day, she agreed to go.

When Shyam’s mother heard this, she was annoyed. She had already told Aaji about the work of preparing and grinding the flour, but now Aaji was saying she had to go to the neighbor’s house for papad-making. Shyam’s mother was angry at her for putting off the work at home. Thinking about all the chores, she said to Aaji, “If you go, how will the flour mixture get done here?”
Aaji replied in a loud voice, “Did I ever promise to do your flour mixing? Does the grinding stone move just because I pull it?”

Hearing this answer, Shyam’s mother’s anger flared up even more. She said sharply, “You can’t do the work at home, but you have the strength to do other people’s work. You go to them and expect to be praised? You can’t pound rice at home, can’t catch your breath, but for others you can pound rice, fetch water with pots—how do you manage all that?”
“Do they really go? All pretenses!”

“I, I work for people. Who are you to question me? I eat what I earn—what I get, I eat. There’s no one else for me. Everyone is the same to me! You don’t understand me! Who are you calling a hypocrite? I never listen to such nonsense from anyone. Yashoda, don’t try to act too clever. Don’t keep nagging me,” Aaji flared up.

“Why did you tell me yesterday to roast the flour? I made all the preparations and then you changed your mind at the last moment, saying you’d go to someone else’s house! I work myself to the bone. And then you won’t even let me touch anything?” Aai said.

“Fine, I won’t touch it, is that enough? But won’t you even wish me well? Can’t you bear to say a kind word to me? What’s so hard about wishing me well? I’ll stop speaking to you then,” Aaji retorted sharply.

Aai exaggerated a little, Shyam thought. But she did feel hurt, and that too he could see. In Shyam’s opinion, some people leave their own household chores to work for others. They are treated kindly by those people, and feel a sense of pride in their work. But it’s not as if they do it out of pure goodness. Rather, they find some comfort in being valued by outsiders. That’s why such things happen. Truly, there’s no real meaning in such work.
These quarrels between Aai and Aaji were a daily affair. They lasted only a short while. All the bitterness in their hearts would spill out, and then their minds would become clear and calm again.

Aai stopped arguing. But Aaji’s muttering continued. “I go and work for others. Who are you to question me? When people treat me kindly, why does it pain you so much?” This grumbling too faded away after a while.

Some time passed in silence. After a while, Aai rose and went to Ajji’s feet. She admitted her mistake. “You are elder! I should not have spoken to you like that. But lately, with all the work, the pain, and the worries, I have been worn out, and at such times, I lose awareness of what I am saying. What is the point of living such a life? Sometimes I feel death would be better! Please forgive me.”

These words soothed Ajji. She understood her. “Don’t say such inauspicious things. You have young children. If you go, who will look after them? Should I send them away to get married? If you speak like this again, I will not be able to bear it. Things look worse after they are torn apart.”
Aai then told Ajji to go and check on the papads. She asked the others to finish grinding the flour. She told Vatan to go and fetch some buttermilk.

After she had done all this, Ajji’s anger faded. Again and again, Aai said, “Don’t be angry over what I said.” Ajji replied, “You too, don’t keep anything in your heart. I am like your own daughter-in-law, your own child. You must forgive me too.”
Ajji went to check on the papads, and Aai got back to her household chores.

Shyam says, “My mother was not faultless. In this world, no human is without fault. Only God is blameless. The Mother of the World has adorned everyone with the ornaments of faults. To err is the ornament of man, and forgiveness is the ornament of God. My mother made mistakes, but she always corrected herself. When she made a mistake, she never failed to recognize her own fault.”
chapters.summary: After an invitation to make papads causes an argument, Shyam observes Aaji and his mother, contemplating the nature of mistakes and forgiveness in their relationship.

chapters.title: The Joy in Sacrifice
paragraphs: School had closed for the Diwali holidays. Immediately after, Shyam returned home from Dapoli. In Maharashtra, the Diwali festival is celebrated with great enthusiasm. People living in Pune and Mumbai come home, bringing with them new clothes, toys, and sweets for their loved ones.

Shyam and his younger brother each received a new shirt from their father. Since the family had become poor, it was not possible to buy new clothes for everyone. The old dhotis had been patched at the edges. The same was true for the cloth of Shyam’s mother. Both brothers were aware that they wore each other’s hand-me-downs. But mother noticed that when the boys went out to play, the younger one really needed a new dhoti.

Shyam’s elder brother was studying at his uncle’s place in Pune. He could not come home for Diwali. From Pune, he sent three rupees and some sweets for the children through a man from the village who was visiting. Mother was overjoyed to receive those three rupees. She gave the children some sweets to eat. They were delighted and started playing in the courtyard.
Mother called Shyam aside. She asked him to go to Amrit Sheth’s cloth shop in the market and find out how much a pair of dhotis would cost.

We went and arrived at the shop. Amritsheti’s children were at the shop. In front of them, I inquired about the price of a dhoti cloth. I chose two or three samples of good quality and soft texture. Taking them home to show, I came back after bargaining over the price. While leaving, Amritsheti told me to return soon after showing them at home.
“Here, here, come back quickly. Once you decide, bring the money,” Shyam said simply, but with firmness.

“What money? Do you have so much? You haven’t even got a broken coin from your father!” Amritsheti said, half in jest, half in pity, thinking of the debt still unpaid. He was still waiting for that money. Hearing Amritsheti’s words, Shyam felt bad. But what could he do? Living with self-respect, Shyam had realized that having debts did not mean being under obligation.

He came home. He showed the dhoti cloths to Aai. She liked one of them. Taking that, Shyam went back to Amritsheti. He took the selected dhoti, paid the money, and brought it home. Aai cut the dhoti into two separate pieces. She pressed the folds with her fingers and set them aside.

Soon, it was the day of Diwali. Bapu had gone out, but he returned home. Aai kept the news of the new dhoti a secret. The children joined in the secret. As Diwali approached, everyone cleaned the house thoroughly. They took out the seeds from fenugreek, distributed the fragrant ubtan to apply on the body, and prepared everything. The children helped with the chores. Dirt, they said, is hell. If you don’t clean away all the dirt, you must kill the demon Narakasura. The women did this work very well. Aai set up a new tulsi vrindavan. She cleaned the lamps, put in new wicks, and made them ready. In the morning, after lighting the lamps, she went around to different places in the house, performing the rituals. Everyone had to get up early, so the children went to bed early at night. Aai, mother...
She was busy working.

Among everyone in the house, Aai was the first to rise at dawn. She lit a lamp in the kitchen. First, she bathed herself. Then, one by one, she woke the children, massaged their bodies with oil, and applied *utna* to them before bathing them. Today, there was plenty of water for their baths, which made her happy. Bhau got up and gathered flowers for the morning worship, making all the necessary preparations. Of all, he bathed last. Aai had already kept the water ready for him.

The children bowed before the household deity. Then, they went to the temple with Aai. Baba, after bathing the younger ones, performed the puja in the temple. He offered *nevariyo* and *modak* as *naivedya* to God. The offerings were distributed among the children. Then, they returned from the temple with Aai.
“Where is my dhotar? I don’t see my towel either,” Bhau asked Aai.
She replied, “I tore it into two pieces to wipe the children after their bath.”
“Then what will I wear after bathing today?” Bhau asked.
“Wear this dhotar today,” Aai said, handing him a new piece of cloth. He was surprised to see it. He asked, “Where did you get this from?”
“I bought it from Amrit Shet,” Aai replied.
“I had asked him for it on credit, but he was not ready to give it. He said, ‘First pay the previous dues, then I’ll give you more. How did you manage to get it?’” Bhau asked.
“I sent Shyam to buy it,” Aai said.
“Where did Shyam get the money from?” Bhau asked.
“I gave it to Shyam,” Aai replied.
“But where did you get the money from?” Bhau asked.
“My brother from Pune had sent me some money for Bhau Beej,” Aai answered.

"Those clothes rightfully belong to you. Your clothes have become threadbare and worn out in many places. Haven’t you the right to those new clothes? Don’t we have a claim over that money?" said Bhau.

"Are you and I really separate? For so many years, we have lived together as one family. We have shared joys and sorrows. How can we be apart? What is yours is mine, and what is mine is yours. You did not get a new dhotar, and I received everything. If I did not get new clothes, what of it? There is happiness even in that. Now you wear it. Why hesitate and touch it with such doubt?" she tried to explain to Bhau with affection.
"If I wear the new dhotar and you do not get anything new, how can I enjoy that happiness? You may find joy, but what about me?" Bhau’s voice choked with emotion, and he could not say more.

"My happiness is your happiness. People will see you in new clothes among others. When do I ever go out? Later, when there is time, I will get something for myself. For now, accept it wholeheartedly. Today is Diwali. Let everyone spend the day in joy," she gently consoled Bhau.

"With a mother like you, who is a lifelong companion and whose children are sweet and precious, what more happiness could there be? Though I am poor, I am richer than all the wealthy people in the world. Then why should I not be happier than all of them? Here, take this dhotar," he said, and put on the new dhotar, bowing before God.

When Bhau wore the new dhotar, the children clapped and rejoiced. But the truest happiness was felt by Shyam’s mother. That happiness could only be experienced by her, for it was the joy born of sacrifice! The happiness that comes from a sacrifice made with love! Its sweetness can only be truly known by living it.
chapters.summary: As Diwali nears, Shyam's mother secretly buys new clothes, leading to a poignant moment where she explains the joy found in sacrificing for her family's.

chapters.title: The Proposal for Marriage
paragraphs: It was the month of May, and the school holidays had begun. Soon after, the season for sowing arrived. Whenever Shyam came home for the holidays, he would help his mother with whatever she was doing. Whether it was grinding grain, fetching water, washing clothes, cleaning the utensils, sorting rice and lentils, or sweeping the courtyard, he never hesitated to lend a hand with any household chore. He felt no shame in helping his mother with the work that needed to be done.

By this time, his mother’s health had begun to fail. Now and then, she would be struck by fever. But as soon as the fever subsided, she would return to her work. There was no one else in the house to help her. So, whenever Shyam came home, she felt relieved. He would assist her with all the tasks, doing whatever was necessary as she instructed. And if, by chance, his mother was bedridden, then massaging her feet was a duty he never neglected.

So it was, one evening. Night had fallen. Everyone had finished their meal. Outside, the moonlight bathed the world in a gentle glow. His elder brother, having eaten, went out. The younger brother went to bed. Mother cleared away the dishes and smeared the floor with cow dung. Then she said to Shyam, “Shyam, there’s a little grinding left to do. Will you help me with it? Haven’t you already done enough digging this evening? Are your hands aching?”

“Aai, my hands don’t hurt at all. Of the four hands, two are still left. When your loving hand touches me, my tired hands find new strength.” Saying this, she spread a sack in the courtyard. She sat down to grind the grain. Mother began to move the grinding stone. Shyam’s favorite sweet, patolyo, was to be made that day, so she had decided to grind the rice herself. In the courtyard, under that clear moonlight, the two of them sat together, grinding. A cool breeze blew all around. In that pure, nectar-like radiance of the moon, Mother began to sing a lullaby for Shyam. As she sang, she wove Shyam’s name into the song. Hearing his name in her song filled Shyam with joy.

Hearing the sound of the grinding stone, Janaki-vayani—a neighbor—came over. She sat down to help with the grinding, but soon got up and left, feeling awkward. She showed her irritation as she left, and later complained to Mother about it.

Mother explained to her, “Oh, she was only teasing you. Why take offense? Why blame someone for helping with such work? And why be ashamed to help? In fact, those who laugh at such work do not understand its value. Don’t you know that God himself helped Janabai with grinding?”
“He did the grinding, washed clothes, and when Namdev’s drum broke, he played the cymbals at the kirtan, and even danced—is that really true, Aai?” asked Shyam.

Mother asked Janaki-vayani to sit down. Then she explained to Shyam, “Shyam, it is indeed true. Whoever works with devotion to God, remembering Him, He helps them—in your form, in Janaki-vayani’s form, He helps me. In many forms, He comes to help.”
“Aai, will I ever meet God?” asked Shyam.
“Those who are virtuous meet God. You must help everyone. Never look down on anyone. Always speak the truth. Only then will you meet God,” said Mother.
“Shyam, what will you do when Buvaji leaves? Study hard. Get a good job and keep your mother with you,” Janaki-vayani told Shyam.

It seemed as though Shyama was destined to become a sage. He had heard that by chanting the mantra ‘Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya’, Dhruva had pleased God. He asked Aai, “Mother, will I find God like Dhruva did?”

“My son, Dhruva had accumulated much merit from his previous births! His resolve was unwavering. Even when his father offered him the kingdom, he did not return home! His detachment was steadfast. You must strive to make your life worthy. One day, God will surely reveal Himself to you!” Aai replied.
Janakivayni told Shyama to let go of Aai’s hand, but Shyama was reluctant to do so. He and Janakivayni began to quarrel.
“You have turned Shyama into a woman!” Janakivayni said to Aai.

“Who else is there in the house to help me? Sometimes the boys must do the women’s work, and sometimes the girls must do the boys’ work. What is lacking in that? Shyama gladly helps with these chores,” Aai explained clearly.
Shyama says,

“I still remember those words of Aai today. For a boy’s complete development, he must learn tenderness, love, the spirit of service, the ability to endure hardship, patience, and to work with humility. Likewise, for a girl’s complete development, she must learn courage, to steady her mind in times of need, boldness, and the ability to manage the household. Only then can one say that their development is complete. This is the true meaning of marriage. Through marriage, a boy learns the qualities of the heart, while a girl learns the qualities of the intellect. Marriage is a sweet blending, a harmonious cooperation of heart and mind, of feeling and thought. When the qualities of a woman are found in a man, and the qualities of a man are found in a woman, that is true marriage. The ideal of humanity is Ardhanari Nateshwar. By himself, a man is incomplete. Likewise, a woman alone is incomplete. But when the two come together, they become two complete beings. It was for the sake of love, compassion, hard work, and service—the qualities of women—that Aai arranged my marriage!”
chapters.summary: While grinding grain with his ailing mother under the moonlight, Shyam overhears a neighbor's comment about marriage, sparking a reflection on the blending of qualities.

chapters.title: The Woman of Resolve
paragraphs: In Indian culture, there are many vows and rituals, and most of them are observed by women. If a woman faces some hardship, she undertakes a fast as a vow. On that day, she worships the banyan tree. She offers as many as 108 items to the deity, as much as she can afford—betel leaves, mangoes, sweets, bananas, coconuts, areca nuts, silk, sweets, sarees—whatever she can manage, she offers. After making the offering to the deity, she distributes the prasad among the women in her community, especially those whose husbands are alive.

Shyam’s mother used to observe this vow. In earlier days, she performed it with great devotion. At that time, there was prosperity in the house. She donated many valuable things. But now, that situation no longer remained. There was poverty at home. She had to think carefully about what she could afford to offer. Yet she did not abandon the vow. What was the point of asking her husband for money when there was barely enough to eat, drink, or wear? How could she ask him for anything extra? Such thoughts would trouble Shyam’s mother.
It was the time of the festival. There was a small bundle of savings. Shyam had come home. It was during those very days—

On Mondays, Uma’s festival would come. Shyam eagerly awaited it and made preparations for the puja to Uma as was his custom. He asked his mother what should be offered to the goddess. Janaki’s mother had told her that a hundred betel nuts should be offered.
“I have already given betel nuts!” said Mother.
“What if you give something else? Only two days are left for Uma’s festival. Give something sweet, won’t you?” Shyam pleaded.
“Sweetmeats, oil—these things are measured out equally for everyone,” Mother replied.
“Then you offer 108 pieces of jaggery!” said Shyam.

“Shyam, there’s no money even to buy salt in the house. Where am I to get money from? Do you think there’s a money tree in our yard? That coins fall from the sky? We are poor, don’t you know that?” Mother explained gently but firmly.

Then Shyam suggested offering 108 mangoes. But Mother said she had already given those. Shyam then asked for 108 tamarinds to be offered. Mother pulled out a few dried ones from the kitchen. Shyam noticed people laughing, and Mother, a little embarrassed, moved aside. She said, “Let people laugh if they want to! What does it matter to them? God does not laugh at anyone!”

“Shyam, God never gets angry. Whatever is given to Him, it should be given with love. Vidura offered Him just a handful of rice, Sudama gave Him puffed rice, Shabari gave Him half-eaten berries. If something is given with love, even if it is very little, it is enough for Him. If it is not given with love, He remains hungry. Whatever is given with love tastes sweet to Him. Whatever is given from the heart—”

Why do you like it so much? Even if I give him 108 pieces of bread, he will sit and eat them all. Whatever you offer to God should be given with devotion. But where is such devotion nowadays? People are not worthy of it anymore.” Mother explained to Shyam.
“Then, Mother, what do you offer to God? Have you decided on anything?” asked Shyam.
“I have decided to offer 108 flowers. Flowers are so pure, clean, delicate, and what else is there like them?” Mother replied.
“Mother, people will laugh at you! And does the priest really take the flowers?” Shyam asked.

“Shyam, what is to be offered is for God, not for the priest. If the priest sees a flower at God’s feet, he may take it. If not, it remains at God’s feet. Whatever can truly be given to God should be given to God,” Mother said.

“Mother, what kind of flowers do you offer? Are there even such good flowers for us? If not, what if we offer tulsi leaves, blades of durva grass, or bel leaves? Why are these leaves also offered to God?” Shyam wondered aloud.

“These leaves are easy to find. They last for twelve months. Flowers do not last like that. They bloom only on certain days. Understanding the difficulties of people, the sages and saints declared that leaves are dear to God. Saints said this so that the poor would not feel jealous of the rich. The rich should not become proud, nor should the poor feel ashamed. This is the meaning of offering leaves. No matter how much money is offered as dakshina, it is not accepted without a tulsi leaf. So, leaves are as important as money. For Ganapati, durva grass comes first, then—
Shankara rang the bell. “I have sometimes offered one hundred and eight tulsi leaves in advance,” said Aai, sharing her opinion.
“Then, Aai, why did you offer flowers at this time? Tell me,” asked Shyam.
“I already told you, son. I offered flowers as a vow. Every day, there are roses and dhavda and champa flowers. If I find fragrant flowers, I bring them,” replied Aai.
“So, did Bhau go to Jalgaon?” Shyam asked.
“Yes, there is a big garden there. He went to gather nagchampa flowers if he could find them. We don’t have money, so we must be willing to work hard. That’s why Bhau went there,” said Aai.

There are many varieties of champa flowers. Among them, the nagchampa looks especially lovely. Its four spotless petals and the golden-yellow pollen in the center are beautiful. Its fragrance is sweet.
Shyam says:

“Even in poverty, Aai held fast to her ideals and lived by them. She would be ashamed and hurt to ask for anything that was beyond our means. She was a woman who taught her children the value of ideals. She was a noble woman who taught us to work hard and trust in God.”
chapters.summary: As Uma's festival nears, Shyam questions his mother about her humble offerings to God, revealing her unwavering devotion despite their family's poverty and hardships.

chapters.title: All Are Equal in the Eyes of God!
paragraphs: There are many castes in Hindu society. Within it, there are countless divisions and distinctions. If you look at the structure of castes, you will see that each branch of this structure is occupied by a different caste. At the very bottom of all these branches, at the lowest rung, are the castes of the so-called untouchables—the Mahars and the Chambhars. Even today, caste discrimination is visible in society. Imagine how intense it must have been a hundred years ago! In every village, these untouchables had their own houses, but they were always on one side, set apart from the rest. Their settlement, called the Maharwada, was always separate. If anyone even touched them, it was considered a great sin.

One day, an old Mahar woman was returning from the fields, carrying a bundle of firewood. As she was passing by a house, the bundle slipped and fell at the doorstep. She sat down right there, exhausted. No one was willing to help her lift the bundle. She waited, hoping someone from the Maharwada would pass by and help her. All this happened before Shyam’s mother’s eyes. The old woman looked very frail. It was evening. Shyam had gone outside to play. When his mother saw this, she called him and told him to help the old woman by lifting the bundle and carrying it to her house. The firewood was heavy, but Shyam did as his mother said, and after helping her, he came back inside.
Let me tell you.

Before telling this, Shyam and I went among the old shepherds. Bhoro showed how to prepare the firewood for cooking. That Bhivan began to cook. “Don’t come here, you Brahmin folk. If anyone comes close, I’ll hit you,” she said.
Shyam, after returning home and bathing, told me this story. Bhoro, who was standing there, was told to go back to his house. He took her and went to Shyam.

This news reached Sridharbhat in the village. He was furious with Shyam. He took out all his anger about learning English. Hearing this, the people from the neighboring house and a lone woman came. She too began to scold Shyam. She let loose all her anger and expressed her rage.
Shyam calmly told them, “I had just gone home to bathe. After bathing, I became pure.”

The old man brought some firewood and gave it to Shyam. Mother took out some rice from the pot and gave it to him. When she realized that he was not well, she understood. Before inquiring about Shyam’s health, she learned that the old man had a fever. But he had to work because of hunger, she said. Mother asked Shyam about the cool fire from the morning. The old man agreed. She took it and gave it to the old man. He sat in the courtyard and ate it. Shyam poured water for him to drink. While eating, he made a small face and said to Mother, “In this world, the poor have no one. May God do you good.”

After this, Mother helped Shyam bathe. She washed his clothes. He remembered a torn story from the past. He said to Mother, “Aai, once I went to eat at Kher’s house. They had puranpolis for the meal. People—”

The wind outside was blowing fiercely. At that very moment, outside the hut, a poor old woman came begging; but no one gave her anything. On the contrary, they drove her away with harsh words. They asked her why she was not ashamed to beg. She was told to wait until after the meal, and then she could have the leftovers. She stood there, trembling, and did not utter a word. One of them, holding a stick in his hand, threatened to beat her. The old woman, dejected and humiliated, went away quietly. These people eat and drink in Irani hotels, and when they come to the village, they show off their status. But when it comes to helping the poor, there is no one to be found. If, by chance, the son of a Mahar becomes a mamlatdar and comes here, these same people will throw a party for him, eat and drink with him, and dance with him, holding him close. How is this just? Money and power are the only gods they worship! That is their religion! That is their deity! The stick in their hands is their only law. But the one who gives that stick is the real culprit! What does this mean? Does God like this? Is money the only god they have?

"My child, in this world, everyone respects only money and power. If a man has money, he is considered great! Everyone honors him. But the God who resides in a poor man’s heart—no one respects Him. No one cares for the goodness of the heart. If a Mahar has no money, we despise him. But if he becomes wealthy, then even people like us—Mahar and Mang—will bow before him. Shyam, if a man is born a Mang, he should help everyone. He should learn to live in society, to follow its customs. Even shaving is a custom! Those who do not have the courage to face the criticism of society are sinners. It is not that they are hated! If we look at it that way, then we are all sinners!" Aai tried to make Shyam understand.
"What you say is true! No one is free from sin. Who can place a hand on their chest and say, 'I am pure'? On the contrary, through suffering—"
Sweat, honest labor—whatever fills the stomach, even if it comes from the toil of the Mahar or Mang, their sweat is just as sacred! To call only the privileged ones virtuous is unjust!” said Shyam.

Mother listened to him with affection. She told him how, in their own home, the women would reap the harvest from the fields, and how people would call them sinners for it. She explained to Shyam how such prejudices were born.
“Aai, since Damaji, hasn’t Lord Vitthal become a Mahar? Didn’t God Himself take the form of a Mahar to save His devotee?” asked Shyam.

“Shyam, all are equal before God! God takes the form of all His children to protect and uplift them. Tortoise, boar, lion, fish—all these forms God has assumed. Why should He exclude any form? God has gone to the huts of the poor. He grazes cattle, He tends horses. He loves Kubja, He honors Shabari. He cherishes Jatayu and Hanuman. The meaning of all this is that everyone is dear to God. For all are His own creation. We call Him God, and to God, we are all beloved. Just as you do what pleases me, so too, you must do what pleases God. He who does not love his own mother and father, his brothers and sisters, how will he love the Mahar? First, learn to love those in your own home. Later, as with Eknath Maharaj, when he took the Mahar’s child into his arms, your love will flow outwards. When love fills your heart, it will reach all, even the Mahar. God belongs to everyone—remember this, and understand it well,” Mother explained to Shyam in her own gentle way.
Evening approached. Mother went to light the lamps, and Shyam ran outside to see who was coming to their door.
chapters.summary: After Shyam helps an old woman from the Mahar caste, his mother explains that God loves all people equally, regardless of caste or status.

chapters.title: Love One Another
paragraphs: Shyam’s elder brother had gone to Pune to study at their maternal uncle’s house. He was very patient and endured much. He studied with great effort, bore everything quietly, and focused on his learning. Pune was an expensive city, so even when the school had holidays, he rarely came home. For one or two years, he would come home only during the longer vacations.

Once, he was struck by smallpox. Smallpox is a dreadful, terrifying disease. When one hears of it, the heart is filled with fear. His whole body was covered with the eruptions of smallpox. Only by the grace of God did he recover, but he was left very weak. After recovering from this illness, he came home during the summer vacation. His body still burned with fever. His eyes were red and inflamed. At such times, it is customary to give the patient cool, soothing foods. Gulkand—made from rose petals—is considered the best, but it is very expensive. Since it was not possible to get it for him, Mother cooked onions with sugar to make a syrup and gave it to him to eat. Onion is said to have a cooling effect. It is also easily available and beneficial.

She would always give the onion sweetmeat to Dada to eat. Shyam noticed all this. It seemed to him that only Dada got to eat it. So he said to his mother, “Aai, you only ever give the onion sweetmeat to Dada. You pour pure ghee over it for him. You give him everything nice to eat. Dada gets everything! If I had a goddess for a mother, maybe I too would get good things to eat.”
These words of Shyam hurt Dada deeply. He felt very bad. He told his mother, “Aai, I feel ashamed to eat all this alone. So from now on, give it to everyone. Am I not grown up now?”

“Oh, are you all stepchildren then? And why do you say such things? Don’t you know he is your own elder brother? Don’t you know that ever since the goddess came, there is light in his eyes and strength in his feet? At night he cannot sleep well, he tosses and turns in pain. The onion sweetmeat is a remedy for his illness. What kind of wish is this, to want the goddess to come just so you can eat well? What is the use of your reading then? Was a person born only to eat? How much love did Lakshmana and Bharata have for Rama! What virtues have you learned from your reading? Would you want your younger brother to die? Leave aside your own brother, you should be ready to serve even strangers. When you go to Dapoli, don’t you apply oil to your uncle’s feet? Don’t you fetch water for him? Don’t you serve him sweet things? Is it right to be jealous of your brother? Before you grow up, will you all become enemies to each other? Shyam, this is not right!” Aai made Shyam understand.

To Dada, she said, “Don’t take to heart whatever Shyam feels. Sometimes such thoughts come to mind.” To please Shyam, she asked him to help her make patolyo. Before she said this, Shyam had gone to the orchard…
The banana leaves were laid out. For the afternoon meal, everyone was served patole again and again. They tasted delicious. Dada himself served kande-pak on the leaves of all the siblings.
While serving, he said to Shyam, “Shyam, do not ask for more patole or kande-pak. Do not cast an evil eye on your brother’s share. Be wise, let them have theirs.”

Hearing this, Shyam’s anger did not subside. He did not go to play with his brothers, and if anyone asked him anything, he replied curtly. Yet, in his heart, he wondered—if there is no love for one’s own brother, how can there be any love left for the trees and plants?

After the afternoon meal, Dada lay down to rest. There was a pain in the soles of his feet. He tried to rub them himself with his own hands, but it only made him more irritable. Shyam always massaged Dada’s feet, but today, even when Dada hinted, Shyam did not go to him. Dada said, “Shyam, you are here, I know. I won’t tell anyone in Pune about the patole. But having to ask you again and again makes me feel ashamed.” In his heart, Shyam longed to touch Dada’s feet, but pride would not let him do so. Dada’s gentle words did not move Shyam.

But Aai, who had heard everything while sitting nearby for the meal, washed her hands and, leaving all her work, came straight to Dada and began to massage his feet. She said to Dada, making sure Shyam could hear, “Why do you trouble him? Is he not your own?” She did not say a word to Shyam. But by her actions, Shyam was softened. Leaving all her household chores, Aai came to serve Dada. What a great heart she had! In her, Shyam saw the very embodiment of love, sacrifice, and toil.

These three—Vagpan, Taga, and Ego—did not remain. I came to my senses and began to work. Then she said to me, “Shyam, let your anger go. Do not take out your anger on her. If you feel sleepy, finish your work and then go to play.” Saying this, she went to her own work. While tending to my feet, I no longer felt angry at Dada. As time passed, Shyam’s anger subsided.

The night’s meal was finished peacefully. The household chores were done. Then, all of them came out into the courtyard and sat together, chatting. The clear moonlight was falling, and Durva’s grandmother was with them. The neighbor Janaki also came and told Shyam’s mother that Shyam should recite the story of Abhimanyu tonight. But she replied that today, Durva’s grandmother would tell the story of Chindhi. Durva recited the verses well. When it came to Chindhi’s story, Shyam felt it was always some old, tattered tale left over. Grandmother began to tell the story.

The story was about the love between Shri Krishna and Draupadi. Subhadra was Krishna’s real sister, but Draupadi was considered one as well. Yet, Krishna and Draupadi shared a deep affection. For many days, Narada had been pondering this in his mind. He brought up this topic to Krishna. To explain the reason behind it, Krishna said, “Narada, I am not indifferent. Whoever calls for me, I go to them. If you wish to test this, then run to Subhadra and tell her, ‘Krishna has cut his finger. Bring a piece of cloth to bandage it. If she gives you one, bring it. If not, go to Draupadi and ask her.’”
As instructed, Narada ran to Subhadra’s house. Subhadra welcomed him and asked the reason for his visit. Then Narada said, “Krishna has cut his finger.”

And then she told him, “Go and tie a bundle of firewood.” She said, “Narada, where do we find such bundles? Look, Shalu, how much he’s grown! It’s no easy task to find a bundle!” When she couldn’t find a bundle, she became distressed. In the same way, Narad went to the spinning room. He told her the whole story. “What? Did you really cut Krishna’s path? Truly? How much did you cut?” Saying this, she too became upset, took the spun yarn, and set aside the bundle. Narad got his answer.

In this way, this incident too, even today, I wonder why it was necessary to tell Shyam about it. She showed the same feeling to him. But Shyam said, “Aai, it was because I acted wrongly towards my younger brother that you felt the need to tell me this story. You always wanted me to love my brother, to be affectionate. You told me this story so that I would feel ashamed of my actions, didn’t you?”

“Yes, but you need not feel ashamed. Rather, you must learn to love,” she said. Hearing this, Shyam immediately got up, went to his younger brother, embraced him, and asked for forgiveness. He promised never to behave like that again. His brother patted him, understood him. Shyam’s pure-hearted nature was evident. He said to his mother, “Aai, we are bound to each other by God’s own ties. Even if we quarrel, we forget it and treat each other with love.”
“Love each other. That alone brings us happiness. Even God is pleased by it,” she said.
In this way, Aai continued to instill values in Shyam, and Shyam was shaped by her teachings.
chapters.summary: After feeling jealous of his brother, Dada, for receiving special treatment, Shyam learns a valuable lesson about love and forgiveness from his mother, Aai.

chapters.title: The Desire to Progress Through Education
