paragraphs: “Whenever there was a fair in Dapoli, I would send Shyam some *pos* (a sweet dish made from coconut and jaggery). He loved *pos* very much!” Mother would say this at home to my elder brother. My brother would reply, “Why should anyone else go to Dapoli? I myself go there, and Shyam would be so happy to receive the *pos* I bring him.”

Shyam had gone to Dapoli to study. While he was there, a cow at home had calved. Mother made *pos* at home. Shyam loved it dearly. Mother remembered her promise to Shyam. Without telling anyone, she took a small container and made some *pos* in it. The *pos* turned out delicious. She packed the container well and gave it to my elder brother. Early in the morning, before dawn, my brother woke up, washed his face, took the container of *pos*, and set out for Dapoli.

When my brother reached the school, it was the mid-morning recess. All the children were scattered here and there. Some were playing games. The children’s chatter filled the air. Shyam and his friend Tagele were playing a game of planting ladyfinger seeds. Shyam was very fond of reading. He was also very fond of memorizing lessons. Because of this, he would often be alone, while the rest of the children would be busy with other things.

He could not bear to lose, even if he was defeated. He would compose verses himself. Because of this, his friends began to call him “Balkavi.” Shyam was lost in play. Just then, a boy came to him and said, “Shyam, someone is looking for you. Where is our Shyam? That’s what they’re asking.” Even as he was saying this, Shyam’s brother arrived, searching for him.

“Brother, why have you come here? It’s time for the bell to ring. I was looking for you at home!” Shyam said to his brother. There was a reason for Shyam to speak so sharply. His brother was now learning English.

Because of this, his friends laughed at him, and he seemed afraid of it. As he began learning English, he started to understand the importance of neat and tidy clothes. He had not yet gained any other understanding. His father’s clothes were rustic—dhoti, coat, and a simple turban. But his father, with all his love, would come here bringing food for his son, and the boy did not yet understand the value of that. The study of English had not yet broadened his mind. On the contrary, it seemed to have taken away some of his good qualities. It was as if his mind had become smaller. He had not yet realized that the growth of the heart is true growth in life. He did not yet understand that there is joy in hard work. He only cared for himself. He only thought of himself.

Father said to Shyam, “Shyam, come home. Your mother has prepared some special milk for you. I have brought it for you. You and your friends eat together. Return the vessel after you’re done.” Brother then called out to his friends for them to come as well.

Shyam had told them that he did not like to eat alone. Eating by oneself is not good. After Shyam said this, one of the teachers took that piece of bread from him. He untied the cloth bundle and called Shyam over. All of them sat together and ate the bread with him. While they were eating, the teacher rested for a while under a tree. The bell rang. The children ran off to their classes. The teacher took the bundle. Telling Shyam to study well, he returned home.

Shyam began to feel ashamed of himself. Seeing such love from his mother and father, he was lost in his own thoughts. He began to feel the pain of his own ingratitude. His father had walked twelve miles carrying that bread, and his mother had sent it with such care and love—how could he ever repay the love of his mother? This question troubled Shyam.
The love he received taught him to give love to others throughout his life. It was through this love that he found happiness in living.

He realized that learning should lead to the growth of the mind. One should not be deceived by outward appearances. One must learn to recognize the qualities of the heart. Through this, a sense of equality is born. The whole world begins to feel like one’s own. One must give love to all the brothers and sisters in the society around us. Only by doing so can we say that we have, in some small measure, repaid the debt we owe to our mother and father.
chapters.summary: Shyam's brother arrives at school with a treat from home, but Shyam's reaction reveals a growing self-consciousness and a potential disconnect from his family's values.

chapters.title: Everyone Should Share in Social Work!
paragraphs: “Samb Sadashiv, let it rain on the fields, let the crops grow, let us sell milk and curds.”
Thus prayed the villagers, pouring water over the Shiva lingam.

Everyone, young and old, was present. Shyam began to recite the mantras. He poured the first kalash of water over the lingam. Then, one after another, everyone took their turn. At that moment, they all became one in their devotion.

In some regions of Maharashtra, the rainfall is often scanty. When the rains fail, the crops do not grow. In Konkan, there is usually plenty of rain. But sometimes, in certain years, it does not rain at all. When that happens, the farmers suffer great losses. In our land, the fate of the crops depends entirely on the rainwater. If the rains are timely, the crops flourish. The village of Palgad was no exception.

That year, the monsoon began well. The initial showers were good. The fields were sown. But then, the rain stopped. Days passed, but there was no sign of it returning. The earth became hard and parched. The seedlings began to wilt. People ran anxiously to the fields, hoping for rain. Whenever a dark cloud appeared in the sky, their hopes would rise, but the rain never came. Life here depends on rainwater. Water is life; without it, everything withers. These words reveal the true importance of water. Love and water—

Because there is a life-giving power in both of these. Water itself is the very form of God! It has no color, no fragrance, no shape. Its greatness is difficult to describe! Anyway, when the rains are delayed, after the monsoon fails, people, following the old tradition, pour water over the Shiva lingam, praying for rain. They immerse the lingam in water and bathe it. The whole temple becomes filled with water. In some places, this ritual of pouring water continues for a week. Yet, even after the rains arrive, the work of pouring water does not stop immediately. This task is divided among the families of the village, each taking turns. All the villagers, young and old, participate in this work.

When the people of the village began the ritual of pouring water over Shiva in the temple to pray for rain, the temple became crowded. The chanting of the Rudrasukt began. Their voices rang out in a grave, solemn tone. Shyam’s father knew this hymn. He too took part in the ritual. Shyam, however, stayed at home. The other children were busy with the same work. Seeing this, Shyam’s mother called him and said, “Shyam, why don’t you go to the temple? You too should fetch water and pour it over Shiva.”
“But, Mother, will the elders let me join them?” Shyam asked.

“My dear, you take a small pot. If that’s too much, take a tumbler. Carry water from the lake, one tumbler at a time, and pour it over the deity. It’s easy to go to the lake. Come, you too should go and help with the water!” his mother explained.
“If I go carrying a tumbler, people will laugh at me,” Shyam complained to his mother. In truth, he didn’t really want to do the work.

“Shyam, do what you are able to do. Do whatever you can, wherever you are. People laugh only when someone tries to do more than their strength allows. Sitting idle like a lazy person is not good. This is for everyone...
Everyone had their own task. Each one had to take a pot and fetch water. To neglect one’s duty was a bad thing, my mother said.

Would one die from doing such work? What harm could it do? Krishna had lifted the Govardhan mountain. The cowherds had offered him their little sticks. Did all their sticks weigh the same as his strength? When Rama had to cross over to Lanka, he built a bridge. Hanuman and the other mighty monkeys hurled great boulders into the sea. But even those who could not lift heavy stones would bring small twigs and throw them into the water. There was a little squirrel, too, who rolled in the sand and carried grains of it to the bridge. Each one did what they could, according to their strength. They all helped in the work. You have read this, haven’t you? Building the bridge was a sacred task. Killing Ravana was for the good of all. In such noble work, everyone should lend a hand. Do as much as you are able. If you can fill a pot, bring a pot; if only a tumbler, then bring a tumbler. I have to tell you all this, Shyam,” my mother would say, her words full of meaning.

These words left a deep impression on Shyam. He picked up a small pot. With all his strength, he joined in the work of fetching water. The chanting of mantras was going on. All the little children from the village were helping to fetch water. One of the priests said to Shyam, “So you have come today? Aren’t you ashamed, now that you are studying English?” But Shyam remained silent. He became one among the children. He joined in their chanting. He began to dance with them. He sang in a loud voice:
“Samb Sadashiv, give us rain! Samb Sadashiv, give us rain! Let the rain fall and fill the fields and streams. Let there be peace and plenty.”

Everyone was praying to God with all their hearts. In community work, there is no place for shame. Do what you are able, with all your heart. Why should you feel shy among your own people? Work as a child among children! Work as a hand among hands!
chapters.summary: When Shyam hesitates to join the villagers praying for rain, his mother inspires him to contribute what he can, leading him to joyfully participate.

chapters.title: To Become Great, Become Virtuous Above All!
paragraphs: “Bhaurao, a five-rupee note is missing,” said Phadkebaba.
“I’ll look for it right away. I’ll search all the bags. Did you give it to anyone?” Bhau.
As this conversation was going on, Shyam, who was in his mother’s room, overheard it.

Soon, everyone had finished their meal. Aai was still eating. On her plate, there was a little rice left. Shyam, noticing this, said, “Aai, is that little rice enough for you? It seems there’s some left over today!”
“My child, I don’t feel like eating much today. There’s still work to do in the house. Somehow, I’ll fill my stomach. I keep waiting for the day when you will become great,” Aai replied.
“Aai, I really will become great. I will study hard. I will read a lot,” said Shyam.

“Study, but become good as well. These days, we see that educated people can also go astray. Even if you get a big position, you may fall. Even if you become great, you may fall; but you must become great in your heart. You must become great through your virtues—that is what I feel. That is what I pray to God for,” Aai answered, her voice sweet and full of love. Though she was uneducated, hearing such noble thoughts from her filled Shyam with wonder.
“Even if you become great, become virtuous.” This reply from Aai was etched in Shyam’s heart.

They beat just as one beats with a whip. They looked as if they had been whipped with a rope. There must have been some reason for such torn slippers. Shyam had developed a fondness for reading books. In Dapoli, he had found many good books to read. Around that time, books by Ram Tirtha had come into prominence. Through a relative, he managed to get hold of one part to read. He liked it very much. He wished he could buy all those books. By reading the old Marathi Puranas, his understanding had grown considerably. But he had no money to buy books. Even the necessary textbooks for his class were not enough for him. He did not have a dictionary either. The books by Ram Tirtha had deeply impressed him. He began to feel that he must have them for himself.

One day, he returned home from Dapoli. At that very time, two guests had arrived at their house. One of them was an acquaintance—a frequent visitor, Balwantrao Phadke. The other was a stranger. In the pocket of the stranger’s coat, there was money—a lot of notes. Without anyone noticing, he took out one of the notes. It was a five-rupee note. He knew that stealing was a sin! But he thought he would atone for this sin by doing the good deed of reading books.

That night, while the guest was counting his money, Shyam was teaching a shloka to his younger brother: “I am greatly attached to you, O ocean of compassion, grant me good intellect.” He was praying to God for wisdom, and at the same time, he had committed theft. The guilt of that theft gnawed at him. That disgrace weighed heavily on his mind.
When the money was counted again, one five-rupee note was found missing. Then Phadke Baba whispered this news into Shyam’s father’s ear.
“There was no one else in the house! Who could have done it?”

“Shyam, think carefully. If someone comes in and tells them, they will find out. Children are often mischievous. These days, children pick up bad habits like smoking bidis and chewing betel leaves.” “Shyam, oh Shyam,” Balwantrao called out to Shyam.

Shyam came and stood there. He was told that a five-rupee note was missing. Shyam replied that he had not gone anywhere outside. He also said that he had only gone out to play. His brother asked him if he had taken the money. Shyam denied it.
Aai came in after washing her hands and sat down beside them. She asked what had happened. Neither of them liked the idea that money had gone missing from their house. Aai looked worried.
“Shyam, are you sure you didn’t take the money? Just yesterday, you asked for money to buy a compass box,” his brother asked again.

Aai, taking Shyam’s side, tried to defend him. “Even if Shyam gets angry, he never touches anyone else’s things. That is his good quality. He doesn’t hide anything. Whatever he does, he tells us. Shyam doesn’t take what isn’t his. And if he ever does, he admits it. Shyam, did you take the money?” she asked gently.

Aai’s trust in her son began to melt her heart. “Shyam doesn’t take what isn’t his, and if he does, he confesses.” These words from Aai struck deep into his heart. Could he betray her trust? Could he break her faith in him? Slowly, tears began to well up in his eyes.

“Shyam, why are you crying? Did I say you took it? I know you never take what isn’t yours,” Aai said. Like ice melting in water, Shyam’s heart dissolved at Aai’s words. Crying, he ran into his mother’s arms and said—
“Aai, did Shyam really take that note? Is this true?”

Shyam could not bear to go near his mother. Aai looked very sad. How much trust she had placed in her child! But now, that pride she had felt for her son had crumbled away. Still, he had not gone so far as to commit the theft entirely, and so there was some relief. He had confessed when asked, and those words were indeed true.
“Shyam, never steal again. Even if it is a small or insignificant theft, do not let it happen. You did well to confess,” she said, gently explaining to Shyam with these words.
Balwantrao too tried to comfort Shyam and gave him a rupee. Shyam gave it to his mother.
“Shyam, why did you take that money?” Aai asked.
“Aai, I wanted to buy more books to read!” said Shyam.
“Oh, but the very first lesson in those books is never to steal! You have read that. Yet you have not truly learned it! Why do you need more books then?” Aai said to him.

Aai spoke simply, but her words carried deep meaning. Sometimes, a single sentence can bring salvation to the mind. Reading or memorizing does not bring true knowledge. Many people read a lot, but do not learn. To learn is to experience. Once you have experienced something, that knowledge becomes firm. Socrates called virtue true knowledge for this very reason. Shyam had read the words “never steal,” but he had not learned them. Truth, compassion, love, non-violence, celibacy—each of these is a small lesson to be practiced. But unless one experiences them, a person cannot be truly born!
chapters.summary: When a five-rupee note goes missing, young Shyam grapples with guilt and Aai's unwavering trust as he faces the consequences of his actions.

chapters.title: You Have Truly Grown Up Today!
paragraphs: It was the time of Ganpati festival. Shyam was supposed to go home. Heavy rains had fallen. Shyam always felt a longing for home. And when one is away from loved ones, this longing only grows stronger. Now, Shyam’s mind was in just such a state. Besides, there was another reason for his eagerness to go home. He had had a new coat stitched for his younger brother. In Konkan, the days of Ganpati are days of great excitement. Those who have gone away for work return home. When they come, they bring new clothes for their family members. Shyam wanted to give that new coat to his younger brother.

In the month of June, while coming to Dapoli, he had made a decision. One of his younger brothers, whose old coat was torn, had insisted on a new one, and at that time, Shyam’s mother had told him, “Your elder brother (Shyam), after growing up and starting to earn, will stitch a new coat for you every year.” This had stayed in Shyam’s mind. In those days, there was no such thing as fashion in clothes like there is now. There were no uniforms either. Everyone wore the same kind of coats and dhotis. If it was not cold, it was hot. The clothes were the same, only the fabric changed. The younger brother’s coat was worn out. Shyam had decided to have a new coat stitched for him for this Ganpati.
It is easy to make a resolution, but to actually carry it out is just as difficult. To get it stitched by Madage...

Success requires effort. Shyama faced such difficult questions with courage. Brother would come to Dapoli now and then for court work. Even though we were poor, these duties were never neglected. Whenever brother came to Dapoli, he would meet Shyama. He would ask about his well-being, tell him to study properly. He would also give Shyama a rupee or two for food and other needs. Shyama decided to save this money. He did not spend a single paisa from it. By Ganapati festival, he had saved three rupees. As the festival approached, he counted his coins in front of Pavana. He bought cloth for a coat. After measuring, he gave it to a tailor. He took his younger brother, a little boy, along, and had the coat stitched to his size. With the money he had saved, everything fit perfectly. Shyama brought the coat home. He was overjoyed. The thought that his little brother would get to wear a new coat for Ganapati filled his heart with happiness.

Shyama hurried out of the house. Rain was pouring down without pause. The path he took was slippery, but he told himself not to worry about such rain. Yet Shyama’s mind was restless. Now he could not remember any warnings. When one is hungry, one finds ways to get food—such thoughts came and went in his mind. He wrapped the coat carefully. On the way, he saw images of home in his mind. He passed a cowshed on the road. It looked warm and inviting. In his hand he carried a stick. Taking the name of God, and leaning on the stick for support, he pressed on. Suddenly, his foot slipped—he fell. But God protected him. The love of his mother protected him. The river was swelling with water, eager to meet the sea, and Shyama was eager to reach home—to meet his family. His feet were torn and bleeding.
A clap of thunder echoed across the fields. Darkness deepened. The rain made the night even blacker. In such a state, Shyam finally reached home.

"Anna has come, Aai! Anna has come!" the younger brothers shouted with delight and opened the door. The brothers sat together for the evening meal. Mother was lighting the hearth. Hearing that Shyam had arrived, she came outside.
"Shyam, why did you come in such rain? Didn’t you find shelter anywhere on the way?" she asked with concern.
"Somehow, I managed to come!" Shyam replied.
"By Ganapati’s grace! Take off those wet clothes and bathe in hot water," Mother said.
Shyam went to bathe. The younger brothers untied the bundle he had brought. Among his things, they noticed a new coat. When Shyam returned from his bath, the little brothers asked him,
"Anna, who gave you this?"
"I’ll tell you later. First, go inside and warm yourselves," Shyam said.
"Aai, Anna has brought a coat. It looks just his size! It’s too small for Anna! It seems meant for me!" the younger brother exclaimed to Mother, full of excitement.

Mother handed Shyam a dhotar to dry himself. Wiping himself, he sat near the kitchen in the warmth of the night, close to Mother. She asked, "Shyam, whose coat is this? Did some neighbor send it for you?"
"No, Aai, I had it stitched for Purushottam," Shyam replied quietly.
"Where did you get the money? Didn’t you lose your fees again? Or did you borrow it from someone?"
“Did you take a loan?” Bhau asked question after question.
“Did you beg from anyone for money?” Aadhyan Bhivn asked anxiously.

“Aai, that day you told me this, and you had forbidden me from ever stretching my hand out for money. How could I forget that? I did not take a loan. I did not let the fees go unpaid. I did not steal,” Shyam explained.
“Did you borrow from the tailor?” Bhau asked.

“Bhau, when you came to Dapoli, the money you gave me for food and other expenses, I saved some of it without telling anyone. With that money, I got this coat stitched. Aai used to tell Purushottam, ‘Anna and Dada have grown up, so they got new coats stitched. He longs for one too.’ I saw that longing, and I made up my mind to get this coat stitched for him. Purushottam, try it on and see how it fits!” Shyam clarified.
“Anna, it fits perfectly! It feels so nice inside. Now all I need is a new pencil. Aai, look!” Purushottam said gleefully, showing the coat to Aai and Bapa.

Listening to what Shyam had said, Aai’s heart filled with emotion. She said, “Shyam, you are not just grown in age, not just in stature or education, but today you have grown in heart. May this love always remain in you. O God, may no evil eye ever fall upon them!”
Bapa gently placed his hand on Shyam’s head. He did not say anything. But that touch said everything, expressed everything! That silent gesture conveyed all the feelings!
chapters.summary: During a torrential downpour, Shyam braves a treacherous journey home, eager to present his younger brother Purushottam with a specially made coat for the Ganpati.

chapters.title: The Pilgrimage to the Sacred Place
paragraphs: In Dapoli taluka, by the sea, there is a small village called Ladghar. There stands a temple of a goddess. Close by, there is a place known as Tamas-Tirth. There, the water of the sea appears reddish. Before taking the goddess’s darshan, people bathe in the sea at this spot.

When Shyam was young, his mother’s joints used to ache. At that time, someone had advised her to make a vow to the goddess there. That vow was still unfulfilled. In those days, there had not yet been much progress in science. People believed that illness was caused by the wrath of gods, and so, in all sincerity, they would make vows to the deities. Now, her joints had improved. Though her strength had lessened, she could still walk about. She did the household chores as she went from room to room. Now, she decided to go to Ladghar and fulfill her vow. From Palghar, she would travel to Dapoli and then to Ladghar. In Ladghar, Shyam’s paternal aunt, Sumatai, lived.

In those days, there were no trains or buses like today. Most journeys were made by bullock cart. Shyam arranged for a bullock cart from Dapoli. Mother came from Palghar to that place. She woke up early in the morning. The luggage was loaded onto the cart. The two of them sat inside, and the cart set off. It was a journey of three hours. After twelve years, Mother was leaving Palghar and stepping outside.

They both sat in the cart. It was early morning. Everything was quiet. The sound of the bells around the bullocks’ necks was sweet to the ears. The breeze softly blew. Shyam lay with his head on his mother’s lap. Mother ran her hand through his tangled hair. Shyam’s hair felt rough to her fingers, so she asked, “Shyam, haven’t you put oil in your hair?” But where was Shyam in this world now? He was lost in that peaceful atmosphere. He did not even register his mother’s question. This was the first time that he and his mother were traveling together like this. In his mind, dreams of happiness fluttered. He imagined himself studying a lot, growing up, and filling his mother’s life with joy. Shyam did not answer, so after a while, she asked again, “Shyam, why don’t you answer? Are you still not asleep?” “Mother, you are caressing me. When your hand passes over my body, I feel everything,” Shyam replied. Mother truly began to gently pat him. She started to hum softly. By now, the forest had awakened. The mynas were calling. The whole road passed through dense woods. Many enchanting, captivating sights could be seen, but Shyam still lay with his eyes closed. Mother sang a lullaby, her lips close to his ear, and he suddenly sat up. The lullaby was like this— In this dense forest, Clear, pure water flows. In my Shyam’s life, May God dwell. “Shyam, why did you get up? Aren’t you asleep? My lap is aching now,” Mother said. “Mother, don’t you pray to God for my life? If you call God, he will come—”
"Then what? Doesn’t God keep watch over everyone? How could I have stayed hidden at such a time?" Shyam asked his mother with innocent curiosity.

Gradually, the village began to appear in the distance. In the gardens, people had started their various tasks. The water in the garden wells was clear and sparkling. The air was pleasant and fresh. Children were on their way to school. At such a time, they arrived in the village. Asking around, they found Sumatai’s house. Mother was overjoyed to see her. After many years, they met each other again. Mother introduced Shyam to her. At that time, Shyam was studying in the fourth standard of English. Sumatai first told them to go and bathe. Accordingly, by carriage, they went to bathe in the sea. Sumatai’s younger brother accompanied them. He showed them the place for bathing. Both of them went into the sea water to bathe. The water was reddish and salty. Mother took some of it as holy water, calling it ‘teerth’, and asked Shyam to take some too. She applied vermilion and performed a small worship of the sea. She offered four annas to the sea. O mighty sea! In your vast belly, there are treasures. Whatever a person offers to the sea, it is an expression of their gratitude. From this great sea, a person can learn a little of the spirit of sacrifice. This is its example.

They changed into fresh clothes and returned home. The meal was simple, but it was delicious. Shyam liked it. Since Shyam was shy among strangers, Mother encouraged him to eat. For his sake, Sumatai had specially made something sweet. Shyam recited a verse for them. Sumatai’s younger brother praised him for it. He inquired about Shyam’s studies with interest. After the meal, they rested for a while. Now Shyam had time to play. In the evening, they all went together to visit the temple.

They worshipped the goddess at the temple. Wooden dolls, small baskets, and bangles were offered to the goddess. After eating nallu, phov, and sweets, they had a picnic in the woods. Everyone enjoyed themselves thoroughly. All the women returned home. Shyam and Aai were hoping to leave for Dapoli in the evening.

Satai insisted strongly that they stay at her place. She made it clear to Shyam and Aai how much she wanted them to come home with her. She poured out her heart to Sumatai. Taking a sapling with them, they set out towards Dapoli. Sumatai, meanwhile, invited them to visit her home as well. Aai gave each of the two girls a rupee. She gave Sumatai a khan (a traditional silk saree). Sumatai came and sat quietly. The carriage was about to set off. The sun was beginning to set. The whole sea, glowing in the sunset, reminded Shyam of Tamasatirth. After a while, they left the village behind. The forest began. Darkness started to fall. In the fields, the stars were visible. The cows were lowing in the distance.
“Aai, when will I ever get to travel like this with you again? I have journeyed with you today. When I walk with you, I feel so much of your love,” Shyam expressed his longing.

Aai replied, “You children will soon grow up and go your own ways. I have wandered to many holy places. I have not yet been to Pandharpur. The courtyard here is my Kashi and Pandharpur! The moneylender is always troubling us for repayment. This household journey is the greatest pilgrimage. In this pilgrimage, I only pray to God to let me die with dignity and honor.” Tears welled up in her eyes. She drew Shyam close to her. With a pleading voice, he said softly, “Aai, please don’t leave us. Who do we have except you? I—”
When you go to study, who will I learn from if not you? May God make you like Tuka!” Saying this, she teased her.
“Whatever God does, He does for the best. You are a gifted child,” Mother said gently.
Shyam had read that if God is pleased, He removes all poverty. But he realized that God had not removed their poverty, and he expressed this doubt to his mother.
Even when difficult days befell them, she would say it was all by God’s grace. Shyam asked her to explain this.

Mother said, “I am uneducated; what do I understand! But it seems to me that whatever God does, He does for the good. When I scolded you in your childhood, it was for your own good, wasn’t it? God is far more merciful than I am. We must trust Him. Whether He gives poison or nectar, our faith in God must remain unshaken!”
At last, Shyam found a way to escape and reached Dapoli village. It was late at night, under the new moon, when they arrived. Mother spent the night awake. The next day, she went to Palghar.

That day and that night remained immortal in Shyam’s life. After that, he never again received such a message from her. Day by day, their troubles increased. These hardships tested her. She learned to make a living out of these very difficulties. To Shyam, it seemed as if God had given him his mother as both a blessing and a curse.
chapters.summary: Young Shyam travels with his mother to fulfill her vow to a goddess, and he cherishes the rare, peaceful moments they share during their pilgrimage.

chapters.title: The Debt Will Be Cleared – Even If It Means Going to Hell
paragraphs: “If, after selling the house and the fields, the debt to the moneylender still remains, then sell your wife to pay it off,” said Vamanrao shamelessly.

Shyam’s mother was eating inside the house. How could such words have failed to shock her ears? She rose from her meal just as she was, her eyes brimming with tears. She washed her hands. Vamanrao and Bhau were sitting together. She came to the threshold of the veranda where they sat, and, standing there with a fierce resolve, she said to them, “If you must leave this house, then leave. But how did you not feel ashamed to talk of selling a woman to pay a debt? Do your tongues have no bones, that you can utter such things? Do you not have wives of your own? Go, and tell the village headman and the moneylender whatever you wish. Take the house and the fields if you must. But I will not tolerate such words again. Announce it in the village square, seize everything, do what you will. But never utter such vile things in front of the children.”
“Very well. If that is what you wish, so be it. If, by the end of this month, the moneylender’s debt is not cleared from your household, then—” Vamanrao stopped. “Bhaurao, your wife—”
“Should I endure such insult?” Vamanrao asked.

“You go inside at once!” my brother said angrily. She went inside and began to weep. My brother then tried to console Vamanrao, speaking to him gently, as one would to a child. He gave him the twenty-five rupees, and Vamanrao left.

All this happened because of the burden of debt. In the beginning, banks like Aai’s had disappeared. When people were in need, they would go to the moneylender, and if they could not repay on time, they would be hounded and harassed. Forget about repaying the principal, even the interest could not be paid. Later, the moneylender would send his men to the house. They would press for payment, threaten, and if the money was not given, they would not hesitate to insult openly. Sometimes, it was even decided to seize the house and property.

In this way, my brother had taken a loan from a moneylender. He was unable to repay it. Not only the principal, but even the interest could not be paid. The situation had become dire. Such was their plight. Once a person falls into the trap of debt, it is very difficult to escape. A person may endure hunger, but should never take a loan. To be in debt is to live in hell. Taking a loan may seem easy at first, but afterwards, it brings only sorrow. One feels like a beggar. Self-respect and honor are lost. One is forced to bow before everyone.
When a person goes to the moneylender, he must behave as if he is a guest. My brother would treat him with respect, offer him a seat, and invite him to eat. He would…
The grinding had to be done with great care. The women and children of the house had to endure many difficulties because of it.

Vamanrao, too, was once sent to collect a debt from a moneylender. One day, he came to our house to ask for the money owed to his brother-in-law. He was seated inside, while my brother had gone to the fields. Before leaving, my brother had told us to give him a good meal. There was no sugar left in the house. So Shyama went to the neighbor’s house, borrowed some sugar, and made tea for him. He bathed, and his soiled dhotar had to be washed and dried. What could be done? When hardships come, one must face them bravely!

When my brother returned from the fields, Vamanrao asked him for the money. My brother first told him to rest for a while and went to bathe. He then inquired with the women about the tea and water arrangements. The women told him that after serving tea, they had washed and dried his dhotar. This made him very angry.

After bathing, my brother came back, performed his prayers, and returned from the temple. Purushottam and the women had made all the preparations for the meal. My brother invited Vamanrao to eat: “If you have taken a bath and are pure, please come and eat!” My brother always observed the rules of ritual purity, but for the sake of the moneylender’s man, he had to bend. What could he do? He was under the obligation of the debt, after all.
While eating, my brother asked Purushottam to recite a shloka. But Vamanrao...
Not a word of praise did he receive for his efforts. Instead, did Bhau plead with them to stay for a meal?
The meal was simple. Both of them ate and then came outside to sit on the porch. Shyam’s mother sat inside to eat her meal. Yet, she could hear their voices from outside.
“Bhaurao, today you have agreed to pay the money for the Kalantare case. You must give seventy-five rupees. Don’t let this opportunity go to waste like last time,” said Vamanrao.

Bhau replied, “By selling rice and bullocks, I have managed to gather twenty-five rupees for you. You think of us as wealthy. Why would I let your money go to waste? Gradually, I will pay it all. Let the children grow up a little! The eldest is studying in college. Do the worms in the dung heap always remain there? One day, they too come out!”

“What are you telling me? Until I get my money, I cannot rest here. You need money to build a new house and to educate your children, but don’t you need money to pay off the moneylender’s loan? If everyone who took a loan did as you do, would the moneylender ever get paid?” Vamanrao retorted shamelessly.

“What can I say to you? To build even this humble house, I had to sell the last of the bangles from my wife’s hands,” Bhau said, his voice choked with emotion. Inside, Shyam’s mother’s eyes filled with tears. She ate her meal in silence, a lump in her throat.
At Bhau’s pleading, Vamanrao only grew more brazen in his shamelessness.
The words were spoken harshly. Hearing them, Shyama’s mother’s heart was pierced with pain. She stepped outside and, after moving away from the household, began to weep quietly.

After a while, Vamanrao, with a stern face, came into the house where the women were. He began to speak, “You women have no sense of what to say and when. Do you understand anything at all? Since morning, I have been behaving so gently for her sake! Do things get done with anger? One must speak sweetly and softly! Today, you have brought this misfortune upon yourself. Do you even realize what kind of talk you let slip from your lips?”

“Listen, it is better to die today than to live a life of such humiliation! Has anyone ever listened to a woman’s words with respect? Let him do whatever he wants. Why should we say anything? Let us get to work. Let us go to the fields. Let us drink water. Let us eat leaves and roots if we must. Even if words that pierce the soul are spoken, we must not listen to them!” the women said.
“It is easy to speak, but it is not so easy to act. Only when the time of suffering comes does one truly understand!” said my brother.
Purushottam came running, hugged mother tightly, and began to say, “Aai, don’t cry. We will do as you say. But please, don’t cry.” He tried to console her. The children silently bore the pain.
Yes, all this was the result of a single debt.
chapters.summary: Shyam's mother overhears a callous suggestion about selling his wife to settle a debt.

chapters.title: Aai, Show Me the Way!
paragraphs: “Aai, what should I do? Until now, you have always shown me the way. Now, too, you must guide me,” Shyam said to his mother with longing.

Shyam returned home to Dapoli from Sakoon. He was unable to pay the school fees. He did not get a fee waiver either. What was once possible had now changed. People still thought, “Shyam is a boy from a wealthy family.” But who knew that he had become poor? Whenever he tried to explain this to the teacher, the other children would laugh at him. Shyam could not figure out what to do, and so he came home to ask his mother for advice. His mother told him to leave school.
Yet, in Shyam’s heart, the desire to study further still burned. He had passed his ninth standard, thanks to his mother. He asked her a heartfelt question—
“Aai, at this young age, is it right for me to leave school? What should I do?”
“You have a brother to look after, and you are old enough to work. If you keep studying, it will cost money. So, it is better to leave school and find a job,” his mother explained gently.

“Aai, must I really take up a job right now? I long to study more. I want to go far in life. I want to bring you happiness. How will that be possible if I start working now?” Shyam said, his voice tinged with complaint.
“Shyam, what worth remains in the pride of the poor? The poor must learn to endure and make do,” said Mother.
“Mother, do you think I will become great? Do you see anything bad in me?” asked Shyam.
“A son must strive to become great. But he should not cause his father hardship. When you cannot depend on anyone else, you must learn to stand on your own feet,” Mother explained clearly.

After saying this, Mother showed Shyam the path he should take. She advised him, “Shyam, Dhruva left everything behind and went into the forest. In the same way, you too must leave home and go. Strive for knowledge as Dhruva did, endure hardships for learning. Nothing is gained without effort. If you learn to stand on your own feet, then bear whatever hardships come your way. Acquire knowledge, become learned, and return home as a scholar. Our blessings are with you. As long as I live, my heart will remain with you. What more can I say beyond this?”

“Mother, should I really go? You have understood what is in my heart. I have heard that in the Aundh State, it costs less to study. There, one can learn by begging for alms. You have already instilled in me the habit of working. In that strange town, I will have no one of my own. Should I go, then?” Shyam asked his mother.

“There is no shame if a student learns by seeking alms. There is no sin in begging when there is no other way. But do not steal. Always take pride in truth. Let go of all other pride. Speak sweetly. Keep a smiling face. Make friends. Never speak harshly to anyone in sorrow. Study diligently. Remember all of us. That memory will show you the right path. Please the Goddess of Learning and bring honor to us. I give you my blessing,” Mother said. Shyam remembered her words.
The lamp of inspiration burned, and so did the lamp of hope.
“Aai, you must get Bhau’s consent,” said Shyam.
“That too I have managed. Do not worry about it,” replied Aai.
That night, as they sat down for dinner, Aai brought up the question of sending Shyam to study at the institution.

“We will have to send him money there, won’t we? Even earning a single paisa has become difficult. Every father wants his children to study a lot. But what can one do? Times have become hard,” said Baba, with a sigh of hardship.
“There, education is free. Shyam can study by seeking alms—madhukari. If we send just enough for his basic needs, that will suffice,” said Aai.
“If that is so, then there is no objection. He has my blessings,” said Bhau.

It was decided that Shyam would go to study at the Aundh institution. Baba had to leave for work outside, so he left one day. As the days passed, Shyam’s mind became filled with thoughts of Aai. The thought that he would no longer be able to come home as freely as before made him sad. If he was not at home, who would help Aai? Who would serve her? Who would insist that she eat? Such questions kept troubling his mind. But then it occurred to him—who am I? God is there to help everyone. He takes care of all. God will help Aai. With such thoughts, he tried to find peace in his heart.

That night, before dawn, Shyam was ready to leave in the bullock cart. Everyone was up and about. Though Shyam kept saying no, Aai packed two bundles for him. She gave him a blanket, prepared some food, and gave him a few simple clothes. That night, everyone had an early meal. Aai served Shyam with special care, but she was not satisfied with the meal.

The cart arrived. Brother loaded the luggage onto the cart. Shyam was advised, “Do not quarrel with your younger brother, help him as needed.” He bowed to God. He bowed to his mother and father. He touched his father’s feet with his hands. Shyam fell at his mother’s feet in the courtyard. He bowed to Janaki Vahini and asked her to take care of his mother. He went back to his mother once more. She told him to take care of himself and stay well. Purushottam made a face at him. Shyam, letting go of that teasing, climbed into the cart.

The cart began to move. As the cart turned onto the road, brother walked along for a while. When they passed by the Ganpati temple, Shyam remembered and stopped the cart. Bapu and he went inside the temple. They bowed at the feet of the deity. Shyam prayed to God for the well-being of his mother and father. He again bowed at his father’s feet. His father told him to take care of himself.

Shyam returned and sat in the cart. The cart started off. Brother went back home. For Shyam, the cart of life had begun its journey. Now, entering this vast world, he was all alone. Taking the inspiration given by his mother, he stepped out. She had told him to go forth like Dhruva; but where was that radiant, resolute Dhruva, and where was he himself? This thought came to Shyam. Different images of himself appeared before his eyes, and tears welled up. Even as the cart passed the outskirts of the village, Shyam was lost in thought. The image of his mother kept appearing before his eyes. With her blessings, Shyam felt as if he had received a protective shield and earrings, like those of old legends. She had taught Shyam how to swim and then set him afloat in the ocean of the world. In this world, he encountered many different experiences. Troubles came his way. In all these, by his mother’s grace, he was saved. He felt that in the journey ahead, it would be her grace that would see him through.
Today, Shyam’s mother is no longer in this world. But the experience of her grace still comes to Shyam, again and again. It comes. Even though mother is gone, her grace remains just the same!
chapters.summary: Torn between his desire for education and family duty, Shyam seeks guidance from Aai, hoping her wisdom will illuminate the difficult path ahead for him.

chapters.title: Broken Pearls Cannot Be Strung Together Again
paragraphs: “Nana, do you sit in that house and listen to such insulting words from those people? Do you answer because others do, or because you want to? Even though I am your daughter-in-law, first and foremost, I am a woman. Does it look good to you when you scold them in front of me, in front of our children? Your fate has been broken by your own actions! Why do you harbor such ill will towards their family? Was it not because they were there that you gave me a home? Let me be known as one with broken fortune. If I have lived my life with dignity and happiness, it is only because of their virtue.

If they ever thought of selling the land, you should not have pained them. What is meant to happen, happens! Broken pearls cannot be strung together again. Why should we cause pain to each other’s hearts? At least, do not do so in front of me. Whatever has happened, those are still your people. Don’t they do everything with the intention that it should be good for all of us? God sees everything. Is it not He who gives wisdom? Instead of coming to our hut and speaking such twisted words, come to give us your blessings. Come to give us your good wishes. Come to give us your love. We want nothing else. Do not scold. Do not give advice—those days are gone. I fall at your feet. Whatever is to happen to us, let it happen. But do not keep speaking ill of them like this.”
Saying this, Shyama’s mother fell at Nana’s feet. Nana lifted her up and said, “Woman, get up. You have always acted according to your conscience. Now, return to your home.”
Don’t light the lamp. What trouble will it cause the old man then?”
“Nana, don’t speak like that. Don’t twist the meaning. Just as I am your wife, I am also a woman of this house. I must look after everyone.”

“I want you to go with me, and he wants you to stay. Fortune has left us. Outsiders have turned their backs on us. Now you too wish to leave? You should come with me out of love. You should meet your own people. Won’t you come?” he pleaded softly, with a hint of desperation.
“No! Now I cannot come! If a woman does not honor her own word, what is the point of her attire?” Saying this, Nana left that very night.

After Nana left, Bapu came to see Shyama’s mother. Shyama’s maternal uncle arrived. He had heard of her difficult situation. He spoke a few comforting words and tried to console her, for that was why he had come. Nana was a learned man. He had a sharp mind for practical matters. He was meticulous in his dealings. A man of policy. But also proud—he always believed he was right. He could not bear to be contradicted. By nature, he was somewhat quick-tempered.

After dinner that night, Bhau and Nana went outside and sat down together. Shyama’s mother was eating inside. Nana said to Bhau, “Listen, brother, I have come to tell you something plainly today. I have told you many times before, and you have heard me, but now things have come to a head. You sold the fields and paid off the Marwari’s debt. Let us pay off the rest of the creditors as well. If you do this, you will be completely ruined. Listen to me.”

“But why are you so worried about my affairs? There are many who give advice to the poor. Do they ever understand their own situation? I am the one who must worry about my own debts,” Bhau replied, a bit resentfully.
“Bhau, I have come because I could not bear to stay away. I wanted to tell you—”

Did I not give my heart and soul for this? Tell me, have I not toiled for it? Even for poor people like us, it is important to have a little land left. In this very village, I have seen families with homes and property, but when their cash was seized, all their relatives turned away from them. Only then did they realize the true value of what they had lost. You are offering that paddy field for fifteen hundred rupees—give it away, and pay off the Marwari’s debt.” Nana spoke, his heart trembling with worry.

“Nana, how can we sell the paddy field? We grew up on that land. We have poured our very lives into it. We dug the bunds, increased the yield. The children are attached to that field. They have planted trees there. They will remember it always. That land is like a part of our very being. When our ancestors could not add to the land they had gathered, at least let us preserve what they left us. Land is like a piece of one’s heart. How can I sell my own heart? Land is like one’s own mother. Who sells their own mother? To sell it would be a sin.” Bhau replied, his voice trembling with emotion.

Nana could not accept this reasoning. He explained his own practical view, “Bhau, can we fill our stomachs with these ideals? If land is so dear to you, would you not buy it from someone else if you needed it? Would you not try to acquire it? Can’t you see that? You preach morals to me, but didn’t you once seize someone else’s land for debt? Didn’t you turn out someone else’s relatives? Did you remember their pain then? People sell land, take their time. By God’s grace, the children will grow up and later buy more land. But how can we manage the land while the debt remains? If the moneylender comes to seize it, all our honor will be lost. Everything will be ruined. After that, what will be left to hold in our fists?”
“You speak of honor lost! If my honor is gone, what honor do you have left?” Bhau retorted.
“If my honor is lost, then I am finished. Will you not come after me?”

K said, “They have sent a seizure order to Amkya’s son-in-law’s house. If your honor is gone, then your honor is gone. Think about it. Why insist stubbornly that only you are right, like a madman?” Nana said.
“If you call me mad, then call me ignorant as well. Right now you have found a chance to insult me,” said Bhau.

“I am only telling the truth. You call yourselves a respectable family, but I have seen your real face. I gave dowry. I sent my daughter to your house, hoping she would have a good life. But honor does not fly away with the wind! Are you really noblemen? Your wife doesn’t even have a single gold bead on her body. She doesn’t have proper clothes to wear. She doesn’t get enough to eat. Is this your nobility? When a moneylender’s servant shouts at your wife from the rooftop, can’t you see it? You’ve lived together for thirty years, but what have you achieved? People have insulted you to your face. You have no wisdom left. Open your eyes and see, but still you have no sense. What should I call this madness of yours? Now, I am telling you, think about it,” Nana said angrily.

All these words, spoken in anger, reached Shyama’s mother’s ears as she was eating in the corner. She listened to them with great pain. When she could no longer bear it, she came outside and, as she had done before, told Nana to calm down. Nana, however, got up in a rage.

She went inside and told Bhau to rest and take care of himself. She suggested applying some oil to his body to make him feel better. But Bhau was angry with her too. So she left. She went and sat in the tulsi courtyard. Tears welled up in her eyes. And she began to cry.
chapters.summary: Shyama's mother finds herself caught between her husband Bhau and her father Nana as they clash over land and honor.

chapters.title: The Humble Visitor Comes Home
paragraphs: “When I told him not to go back to study, I saw him come home like that. He stayed at home for about a month. Had the school not reopened yet? Maybe the plague was another reason,” said my brother to his wife, as he gathered cow dung cakes with care.

“Why are you so upset about it? Even if he has to struggle a little, he must go back. He cannot stay here just because there is food to eat at home. And even if he did stay, I would not let him remain idle,” my mother said, taking Shyam’s side.

“When friends say they can get him a job in the railways, if he gets a job there, that would be good. These days, where does one easily find work? You and your son should accept what comes,” said my brother.
“He is still so young; I don’t want him to start working yet. He has a desire to study. He has come here only for a while. He is not the kind to sit at home and do nothing!” said Aai.

“You always see only the good in your children. But sometimes what we say turns out to be true. He came home only because the times were difficult. One day, the truth will come out. You’ll see,” my brother was not ready to give up his argument.

Shyam and his younger brother, while chatting together, both fell asleep. Suddenly, Shyam had a dream and woke up. He heard his brother talking to their mother in a low voice. Listening to his brother’s words about himself, Shyam could not remain lying there. He got up and told his brother, “Brother, I was lying here quietly, listening to what you were saying to Mother. Suddenly, I woke up and heard your words. I came home only because there was plague in the town. But you do not trust me. I did not come home to eat or to sit and eat. Truly, I had no money to go anywhere else. I had to stay here. But the other students there started to avoid me. That’s why I had to come home. Let it be. Whether there is plague there or not, I will leave tomorrow. Just give me ten rupees for expenses.”
“Shyam, do not take your brother’s words to heart. If there is plague there, let it be; you can go later. Listen to what I say,” Mother said.
“I will not stay now. If I am to go tomorrow, I will go. Do not worry. God is there. He saves; no one can kill whom He protects,” Shyam replied to his mother.

“You are so stubborn! Just like your father! Go then. If you stay well, it is good. If you slip from my hands, so be it! God gives such precious children and then makes us weep by taking them away,” Mother said, wiping her eyes with the edge of her sari.

Shyam’s younger brother, Sadanand, had died during the plague. That sorrow still lingered in Mother’s heart. She had heard that the plague had spread to Aundh. Shyam had gone there to study, and so she was even more anxious. The pain of Sadanand’s passing had not yet lessened for her.
This news reached the ears of Aai. Upon hearing it, Shyam was filled with longing.

Due to the plague, the school in Aundh was closed. It remained shut for two or three months. Orders were given for the boys from outside to return home. When it was time for Shyam to go home, he had no money. He sold his blanket and his books. With the money he got, he set out for home.

Shyam got down at the Harne port. He hired a cart and reached Palgad. He walked up to the house at the edge of the settlement. Everywhere, there was silence. As Shyam called out at the door, he stepped into the courtyard. From inside, Aai, straining to hear, asked, “Who is it?” Hearing her voice, Shyam waited a moment on the porch. When Aai asked again, “Who?” Shyam replied, “It’s me, Shyam.” She hurriedly opened the door. She held Shyam tightly. Her heart was filled with relief. She asked him first to bow at the feet of God. She showed him how much she had worried for him. As she spoke of Sadanand’s passing, her eyes filled with tears.
Before his brother, who had gone to the backyard, could return, Aai called out, “Did you hear? Shyam has come. Our Shyam has just arrived.”
Before his brother, who was washing his feet outside, came in, Shyam greeted him respectfully.
“I prayed to Ganpati for your safe return. Did you come safely? Sadanand is gone,” said his brother, wiping his eyes.

“Shyam, it’s still cold outside. Lie down for a while with me,” Aai said. Shyam took off his clothes, washed his face, and lay down beside Aai. She wrapped him in her old quilt. The quilt was worn, but Aai’s love was warm. Lying in his mother’s arms, he felt as if he had bathed in her affection. That night, lying beside her, he kept thinking how fortunate he was to be in his mother’s embrace.
When the memory of a mother’s love comes, the heart fills to the brim.

Shyam had come home and stayed for a month. He and his brother Purushottam would sit together and chat endlessly. Purushottam would tell him stories of what had happened in the village. Shyam would share tales of what had occurred in Aundh. Both would delight in each other’s stories.

One night, lying in bed, the two continued their chatter. As they talked and talked, they both drifted off to sleep. In the middle of the night, Shyam awoke from a dream and heard—his mother and father were still talking. Shyam, hearing his brother’s sharp retort, asked his mother to tell him again the story she had started before. Though she understood, she was not ready to tell it again. She said, “Even if I go today, for a few more days you will still be children. Then, you must tell my stories to others.”
Finally, his mother promised to tell him the story. She never withheld her affection. She never bound her love with restrictions; instead, she gave freedom, she gave independence.

Upset with his father, Shyam left the house to sleep outside. Tears welled up in his mother’s eyes. One child had already been lost to plague, and now the other seemed ready to leap into the same danger. In the quarrels between father and son, her condition became like that of a thread caught in scissors.

Before leaving, Shyam fell at his mother’s and father’s feet. Both blessed him, saying, “Go well.” Unfortunate Shyam left, unable to listen to his mother’s words as he went out the door. That was the last time he saw his mother. He never again got to run into her arms. But he did not realize then that this was their final meeting. Never again did he hear those sweet, nectar-like words from her lips.
chapters.summary: After returning home due to the plague, Shyam overhears a conversation between his mother and brother.

chapters.title: The Day of Fever
paragraphs: “Goddess, grant me the death of a fortunate woman while my honor is still intact.” Shyama’s mother prayed thus to Tulsi on the day of Tulsi Vivah. Why did she ask for this on a festival day? But the circumstances were such.

How much does God test a person? They say that when misfortune comes, it never comes alone. The storehouse of happiness in Shyama’s home was emptied, and the storehouse of troubles began to fill, one after another. Yet, the strength of mind in this household did not diminish by even a hair’s breadth. On the contrary, as the days of fever and hardship increased, their resolve grew stronger. Still, they tried to spend their days with calm and patience.

Difficult days had come upon this family. Each day brought the question—how will we get through today? Yet, the effort to live with dignity continued. If there was oil, there would be no salt; if there was salt, there would be no chili. There would be no firewood for cooking. The children would gather dry leaves and twigs to cook the meal. If there was no fire at home, they would have to go to a neighbor’s house to get a burning ember. What else could she and the others do but strive to live each day with honor? Tatu had left, saying he would return soon, but he did not come back.

Deserted. The house was locked up, and people had left for Pune or Mumbai for the sake of their children. There was no one left in the ancestral home. Shyam’s mother could not step outside the house. For one, she had to maintain her dignity, and secondly, her body no longer had the strength for such things. Day by day, she grew weaker. Shyam had left in anger. He must have been upset with her. Even so, Shyam’s mother would remember him and be filled with sorrow.

At such a time, a pensioner’s family came to live in the village. In truth, they were not originally from this village. They had no relatives or close acquaintances here. But the water of the village, the air, suited them. The people of the village were good. And above all, they had great devotion and faith in the Ganpati of this village. They took a small room near Shyam’s house and built a little bungalow beside it. The husband and wife lived there together. They were both good-hearted people.

Shyam’s mother gradually became acquainted with them. The wife, Radha-bai, was the pensioner’s wife. She was by nature loving and affectionate. The two women would share news and stories with each other. Radha-bai came to know about the poverty in Shyam’s mother’s home.

One day, Shyam’s mother said to her, “Radha-bai, if you have any work that needs to be done, please tell me. If you need grain to be ground, I will do it for you. That way, I will earn a little help for myself.” Radha-bai gladly agreed. She was a woman from the city, not used to such work. She was accustomed to paying someone to grind her grain. So, Shyam’s mother would take Radha-bai’s grain and bring it home. In the morning, after her brother had left for work, she would set up the grinding stone and begin. Sometimes, Purushottam, who was still in school, would help her. Later, she had to do the work all by herself. She would pause often, but still managed to finish the grinding. While she worked, memories of Shyam would come to her. That home—

While she was there, she would help out with such tasks. The three of them would come to the grinding room together. By doing such hard work, she would save a little from the household expenses for oil, flour, and other necessities, and thus help to run the household.

Diwali was approaching. She wondered how to celebrate it in such difficult times. Everyone else celebrated the festival with hope and joy. In the old days, hundreds of lamps would be lit at Shyama’s house. Oil was spent by the maund. But now, those days were gone. Shyama’s mother said to Radhabai, “You must have a lot of work—if you have clothes to wash, shall I do it for you? If there is any work, just tell me.”

Around that time, Radhabai’s midwife, Indu, came to the house. She was not well. She had grown weak. The change in weather had not suited her, and she had to be brought over quickly. Someone was supposed to come and rub oil on her body. She said, “My midwife Indu is here. Can you manage to rub oil on her? And can you bathe the little children, rubbing oil on them as well?”
“I would be very happy to do this. I like such work. When my own midwife Chandrakala was here, I used to rub oil on her too,” said Shyama’s mother.

Early in the morning, Shyama’s mother would go to rub oil on Indu. After that, she would begin her grinding work. While rubbing oil on Indu, it seemed as if she was rubbing oil on her own midwife. She did her work with care and devotion. She would bathe the little children, looking after them tenderly. She found great joy in these tasks. Within a few days, there was a change in Indu’s health. The woman who had become so frail now began to recover.

The lamps began to be lit. Little children could be seen filling the courtyard. Radha-bai felt the difference. Shyama’s mother had developed a deep respect for her. She could not bring herself to go further, so she took out two rupees and gave them to her. Receiving those two rupees brought her great joy. She said, “This is more than enough! Even one rupee would suffice!”

Radha-bai replied, “Yashoda-bai, this is not the price of your work. I must give you something for your effort. You work with such dedication. That cannot be measured in money. Now, Diwali is approaching, isn’t it? Please, accept these two rupees.”

Shyama’s mother returned home. She felt as though God Himself had protected her honor. She bowed before God in gratitude. With that money, she bought oil, ghee, and new clothes. She prepared festive sweets. On Diwali day, she lit two lamps. Purushottam celebrated Bhau-beej. He went to Indu’s house. Indu welcomed him warmly and gave him four annas.

In return for the “fogona” (ceremonial gift), Shyama’s mother gave Purushottam a small bowl and a pair of slippers. He was very pleased. He neither got angry for being given “fogona,” nor did he sulk. Such an understanding child he was.

Diwali passed. The Tulsi wedding arrived. Purushottam brought amla and tamarind. Sweets were prepared. The Tulsi wedding was celebrated. While applying turmeric and kumkum to the Tulsi plant, she prayed with all her heart that death would come to her only after her duties were fulfilled. Now, she could not bear to leave her children. How much work did one person do? She barely managed to feed her children. Gradually, her strength began to return. After enduring days of fever, she started to feel that perhaps her end would come only after she had fulfilled her responsibilities.
chapters.summary: As Diwali nears, Shyam's mother finds solace in helping others, but during the Tulsi wedding, she prays for death after her duties are fulfilled.

chapters.title: What We Feared Most Came to Pass!
paragraphs: “There’s a seizure at Purushya’s house, a commotion!” The children came running from the school, chattering to Purushottam and the others. He hurriedly took leave from the teacher and rushed home to ask what had happened. The adults simply widened their eyes and said, “What is there? The school is over, that’s all.” Purushottam stood there, confused. I found it hard to explain everything to him.

My brother had taken a loan from a Marwari moneylender. The burden of that debt, along with the mounting interest, had become too heavy for my brother to bear. For some days, the Marwari’s men had been coming and hurling harsh and insulting words at my mother, demanding repayment and accountability from her. Shyam, unable to bear this humiliation, once confronted them and asked for an explanation. The Marwari grew furious and began to threaten us with legal action.

The Marwari would not relent. Finally, he filed a complaint in court. Including the principal and the interest, the sum had reached four thousand rupees. He submitted a petition to the court demanding that the amount be recovered from us. The court accepted his plea and ordered that all of my brother’s property and possessions be seized.

With the threat of seizure looming, we were on the verge of being thrown out of the village. When this news reached Shyam’s mother, it struck her like a bolt of lightning. She lost all desire to eat even a single morsel. Two...
She neither ate nor drank anything. She did not sleep. She kept repeating the name of God without pause.

A peaceful death seemed good to her. She prayed to God, “O Lord, grant me only this: let me be able to see with my eyes and hear with my ears until the very end. After that, take this life of mine. I have no desire to live in this world any longer.”
Purushottam went to school. His mother, gathering her strength, must have waved him off with her hand. Tears welled up endlessly in her eyes.

Around nine in the morning, the village drum began to beat, announcing the seizure of property in the village. The drum-beater stood at different places, beating his drum and making the announcement: “Today, the property of Bhaurao’s house will be seized!” Hearing this, Bhaurao’s family felt deeply pained. But there are always those who take pleasure in others’ suffering; such people were secretly delighted.

As the drum-beater made his rounds, he came near the school. The children heard the announcement. The children began to tease Purushottam. Purushottam was still very young. He did not understand the meaning of all this. The whole place was filled with chaos and confusion.

It was ten o’clock when school was dismissed. The children gathered around Purushottam, teasing and mocking him. The fate that befalls a goat caught among wolves now befell Purushottam. Crying, he ran home. Standing before his mother, he began to say through sobs, “Aai, the other children are teasing me. ‘Your house is going to be seized. The gods made of cow-dung are being taken away.’ That’s what they say. Why are they teasing me? Are we being thrown out of our house?”
“My son, God’s will! What can I tell you?” Saying this, she quickly took Purushottam in her arms and began to weep. Both were overcome with sorrow. She then—
Wake up, Sangale, come, wash your hands and feet. Today, let us go to Radha-bai’s house for a meal. Indu, you too come with us.”
The innocent, ignorant Purushottam understood nothing. Since mother said so, I went with Indu to her house.

That day, brother did not eat. He had bathed. He performed the daily worship at the temple. After reading the Ganapati stotra, he went to pay his respects and returned. But all this was done in a daze, as if he were not truly present. He did everything with his head bowed low. Once, in that village, how much respect they had! They were Sardars! They were Panchayat members! But today, none of that remained. People now asked after them with pity. Even the little children now made jokes at their expense. Where once there were flowers, today only dung was scattered.

Mother, with great hardship, had managed to keep up appearances for so many days. Yet, God still put her to the test. Whatever happiness she had was snatched away. Now, God made her endure just as much sorrow.

One day, the moneylender came to Shyama’s house, bringing with him the police, the clerk, the village officer, and witnesses. After the meal, four women hurriedly gathered all their belongings and put them in one hut. Everything—whatever was left, whatever was gone—was thrown into that hut, and then they locked it. They sealed it. They were allowed to keep just two huts for shelter.

After all this, they left. Mother stood there for a long time, rooted to the spot. Her body trembled, but inside, her heart was burning with anguish! She was terrified, shaken to the core. In front of everyone, she collapsed to the ground with a thud and lost consciousness.

“Mother, Mother!” cried Purushottam, weeping. Brother lifted her up and gently rubbed her hands and feet. After a while, she regained consciousness. She said, “What I feared most has come to pass. Now, living and dying are all the same!”
chapters.summary: After the devastating news of the property seizure, Shyam's mother collapses, overwhelmed by the family's misfortune.

chapters.title: Nimaane’s Illness
paragraphs: “Because of me, you are all going through such hardship. You have to feed me, give me water, and look after me day and night, and yet I am of no use to you. I am truly unfortunate! What can I do?” Nimaane said to his wife, his voice heavy with sorrow.

“What are you saying? If you lose heart like this, then on whom will Purushottam rely for support? How can you give up your courage? You must not let your mind be troubled. In your home, I have enjoyed every happiness. You have never let me lack for anything. Now, even if these are days of poverty, so be it. I have never longed for those days of prosperity, and even if I did, you have not been able to bring them back. But with my own eyes, I have seen those happy days, and my soul is content.”
“You are a good woman. Isn’t Sakhu coming? She will take good care of you,” her husband said, trying to comfort her.

“Why should I show any more false hope? All this strength is hollow from within. If, while you are still here, death comes to me and I die in your arms, then my life will have been fulfilled. In the form of a wife, I have found salvation. That is the greatest happiness, the greatest joy. In difficult times, it is thoughts of you that come to my mind. After I am gone, who will you have for support?” As she said this, she placed her trembling hand on her husband’s knee. Her body was burning with fever. Even as she spoke, she was truly—
She asked her brother to give her some water. He gave her water to drink.

"The water from your hands is like the sacred Ganga, the pure Ganga, sweet as nectar itself. Today, do not go anywhere. Just sit by my side. I will close my eyes and think only of you," she said, taking her brother's hand in hers and closing her eyes. That scene was as if the very water of the heart was flowing out.

When the house and property were seized, Durva's grandmother was not at home. Who knows where she had gone. She returned, and that very day, she fell ill and was bedridden with a high fever. Who was there to care for her? Grandmother did whatever she could manage. When grandmother went to eat, there was no one to take her food to her, so she asked Purushottam to stay in the house. The neighbor Radha-bai, Janaki-vahini, and Namu-maushi would come and help with whatever little chores they could.

Now, all work had come to a halt. Even the few coins that came in had stopped. Because of this, everyone in the house felt the pinch of want. When Durva's grandmother was at home, everyone would vent their anger on her. Bhau would calm everyone and say to her, "Dwaraka-kaku, cook the nikhate rice and serve it, but do not make a fuss. Our honor is already lost. Do not add to our troubles."

That day, Aai asked Purushottam to take Indu and send a postcard to Afu. She told her everything—about their troubles, and asked her to write a letter to her elder sister. Now it seemed as if even that last support was slipping away. She told Indu everything. As she said, Indu wrote the letter and addressed the card, and Purushottam was told to drop it in the postbox. Indu, after doing this, returned home.

Aai then asked Purushottam for water to drink. He gently put the water to her lips. Just then, Janaki-vahini arrived. She inquired about Aai's health and hurried to massage her feet. But Aai only asked her to sit by her side. She went home with Purushottam.
He had sent the boy to the barber. The boy brought it back, and I put a small morsel into mother’s mouth. I sat beside her. But mother sent the boy outside to play.

In the evening, Namumaushi came by. She was mother’s childhood friend. She had been given in marriage to this very village. The two of them chatted together for a long time. She would often come to visit Shyama’s mother. Her health was not what it used to be. Her feet would swell. Whenever she came, Shyama’s mother would inquire after her health. Later, Namumaushi asked after mother’s health. She touched mother’s wrist and said, “You have no strength left, have you? You’ve become so frail!”

“Namu, send some clarified butter to your husband Purushottam and a little oil for him as well. There’s not a drop left in the house. Dwarakakaku is growing old. There’s no need to tell you. You understand everything. You know what it is to be poor. But you are not a stranger to me,” mother told her.
“All right, I’ll send it. Don’t worry. You take everything so much to heart! That’s your real illness. Take care of the children. Be brave. You will get better,” Namumaushi said.
“There is no wish left to live now. I have endured enough,” mother replied.
“Don’t say such inauspicious things at dusk. Wait, I’ll cook some rice gruel and bring it for you,” Namumaushi said.
“There’s no more shame left in this life. It’s better to close my eyes,” mother said, closing both her eyes.
“Why do you say such things? You will get better. You will see good days again. Gajanan and Shyam are growing up. Has Gajanan found a job?” Namumaushi asked.
“Gajanan has found a job a month ago. But he gets only nineteen rupees…”
Salary. What he earned in Mumbai, and what he sent here? For teaching. He sent five rupees. He kept only a little for himself, and sent the rest to me,” Mother explained.
“Did Shyam understand this?” Aunt Namoo asked Mother.

“He doesn’t need to know all this, I said. He is always busy with his studies there. Why should we burden him with such worries? Should he come and go, spending money for no reason? Does money grow on trees for him? He comes only when it is truly necessary. Now, he doesn’t have that money, does he? May God keep him happy if He so wishes,” Mother replied.
Aunt Namoo took leave of Mother and returned home.
The letter that Aunt had sent by post was read aloud to Mother by Purushottam. Aunt’s handwriting was neat and beautiful. She understood everything as soon as she saw it. Mother felt a quiet joy.

Just then, Indu arrived. She too read the letter. She felt a longing to meet Aunt. Indu went home and invited Purushottam to come eat and drink at her place. Mother told him to go. The two of them left together.

While brother was still there, Radha-bai came to visit. Brother got up and went outside. Radha-bai had already heard from Indu about the letter’s arrival. She expressed her happiness upon hearing the news. She said, “When there is love in the heart, everything turns out well.”
“You all have loving hearts. What else could it be?” Mother said to Shyam. After sitting for a while, Radha-bai went home.

“Aunt arrived in a bullock cart from across the river. Everyone was eagerly waiting for her. Purushottam and brother brought all her belongings into the house. Purushottam, who had been dozing in his dreams, woke up when he heard that Aunt had arrived.
She came.

“You’ve come? My wait has ended!” said Aai. Aunt came and sat beside her. Aai was only half-conscious. The two sisters were meeting after many years. Seeing each other in such a state, both struggled to hold back their tears. She called out to her sister, “Akka!”

“Sakhu, you’ve come? I was waiting just for you. I wanted to hand over the children to you. I wanted to entrust them to your care. I longed to wrap them in your sari’s pallu and send them with you,” saying this, she began to weep.

“Akka, why do you speak like this, as if you’re leaving us? Haven’t I come now? You are getting better. When you start feeling well, Purushottam and I will take you with us. I am working now,” said Aunt.

“There is nowhere left to go now. Now, I must only go to God. I am just waiting for death in this old hut. I had this house built by telling him. Here, on this very cot, I pray to God that death comes to me while you are all around me. There’s a saying, ‘Let the mother die, let the aunt remain.’ Let that come true. Sakhu, you have no children of your own. Who knows why God made you so attached to my children! Now, you must become their mother,” Aai expressed her wish.
“Akka, don’t say such things now. If you speak like this, you will feel troubled. Now, just rest quietly. I will sit here and comfort you,” said Aunt, and she covered Aai with a warm quilt.
Aunt truly comforted Aai. Ganga and Yamuna had come together. That sacred confluence had taken place.
chapters.summary: As Shyam's mother Nimaane grows increasingly ill, her loved ones gather, and the arrival of a long-awaited aunt brings both comfort and unspoken anxieties.

chapters.title: All in Loving Care
paragraphs: “Why is the cat meowing so much? Did you feed it today?” Aai asked, hearing the cat’s voice from the courtyard as she lay on her sickbed. It was her favorite cat, a gentle creature. It never put its mouth to the milk pot without permission. A little milk was always enough for it.

“Aakka gave it some rice. But it didn’t let its mouth touch the food. Milk and ghee were mixed in the rice, but it just sniffed at it and turned away. Even the fish that was left over, it didn’t eat. It doesn’t seem to want to eat anything,” Sakhu explained.
